title: Melissa Rivers on Her Glorious Return to the Emmys Carpet, Remembering Her Mom Joan and Why ‘It’s Been Really Hard’ to Watch ‘Hacks’
full_text: Sep 13, 2026 6:25am PT Melissa Rivers on Her Glorious Return to the Emmys Carpet, Remembering Her Mom Joan and Why ‘It’s Been Really Hard’ to Watch ‘Hacks’ By Daniel D'Addario Plus Icon Daniel D'Addario Chief Correspondent DPD_ Latest Courteney Cox on Her TIFF True-Crime Drama ‘Evil Genius’: ‘The Story Is So Unbelievable’ 21 hours ago Antonio Banderas, Trudie Styler and Eva Birthistle on the Sorrow and Joy of TIFF Medical Dramedy ‘Up Against It’ 22 hours ago Lee Pace on Romancing Sandra Bullock in ‘Practical Magic 2,’ Life as a Leading Man and His 6-Foot-Five Star Power: ‘I’m a Monster!’ 3 days ago See All Chris Pizzello/Invision/AP/Shutt Melissa Rivers is returning to the red carpet. Fashion expert and author Rivers — who rose to fame reporting outside awards-shows with her late mother, the comedian Joan Rivers — will be joining Variety co-president and co-editor-in-chief Ramin Setoodeh and CNN correspondent Elizabeth Wagmeister at the two brands’ Emmys pre-show broadcast. On “CNN & Variety Red Carpet Live: TV’s Biggest Night,” streaming live beginning at 5 p.m. ET on Monday, Sept. 14 at CNN.com/Watch and on the CNN app for CNN’s streaming subscribers, Rivers will provide interviews and commentary. Related Stories 'Being Heumann' Review: Siân Heder's First Film Since 'CODA' Is a Bold and Stirring Dramatization of the Protest That Launched the Disabled-Rights Revolution 'A Good Little Soldier' Review: Alba Rohrwacher Goes Corporate Drone in Stéphane Brizé’s Lukewarm Workplace Drama Her presence promises to be both a nostalgic look back and a turning of the page, as Rivers insists she wants to strike a tone that’s been absent for a while: As a duo, the Riverses broadcast for E! and for the TV Guide Channel before, in 2007, their association with the red-carpet ended. In 2011, the elder Rivers declared “We’ve done that. It’s not fun anymore.” Melissa agrees, and is hoping to bring a spirit of joie de vivre to the proceedings. The pair continued to host E!’s “Fashion Police,” which Melissa continued after her mother’s 2014 death until the show’s final episode in 2017. Popular on Variety A few days before her hosting gig, Rivers spoke to Variety about the spirit of “fun” she feels has been missing from the carpet, what she thinks of Jean Smart’s performance as a groundbreaking female comedian and what Joan Rivers would say about celebrity style in the age of Ozempic. You’re back on the red carpet after a long absence. What does it mean to get to come back? Well, first of all, it’s my first time back in 20 years. It’s crazy. I’m going to give you the timeline: I was originally supposed to join in via Zoom, and do some color — some fun. Then I got a call either Saturday or Sunday [Labor Day] weekend, and they said, “Would you be interested in being on the carpet?” Without really thinking about it, I said “Sure.” And then 10 minutes later, I was like, “Oh my God!” Suddenly, it dawned on me, I haven’t stood on a red carpet for coverage in 20 years. It became very overwhelming, because I realized I had so much to do. What does your preparation look like? Luckily, I’ve seen most of the shows. CNN gave me a huge briefing book, and I’m going through the storylines, the actors, the different categories, finding interesting facts. The other day, they’re like, “And here are the presenters!” and I’m like — Oh, God, they have to put more in my brain. How I used to do it came back: By storyline, category, and then individuals. Matthew Rhys has won for [“The Americans”], and this is his first time for “Widow’s Bay.” If I end up talking to him, I’m like, “Is there one that you’re more emotionally attached to?” You’ve won, and here you are with your hat in the ring. And with you and Keri Russell — who gets more mirror time? Right — they’re prepping together. Do you do your fittings at the same time? For my wedding, trying to get my husband, my son, and his two sons coordinated for a fitting, it might as well have been D-Day. But I’ve been really outspoken about this: The fun has been gone. The lightness has been gone. It’s not going to be the same as me and my mom; it’s never going to be that again. But there’s a whole new lane for just being fun and lightening up. I’m going to be the shallow end of the pool. Don’t come to me if you’re going to want to make statements. I want to know who you’re wearing, and fun stuff. I want to know, was there ever a performance you really thought you were going to get nominated for, and you didn’t? It felt as if in some point since you and your late mom left the red carpet, the tone of coverage did get more serious. I’m curious what you made of that as an observer. Yeah, it got very, very serious. The one with #MeToo and all the women wore black [the 2018 Golden Globes, at which all female attendees wore black garments in an organized protest], that was great, because there was a theme. Everybody was wearing black, and you got to see actual personalities come through, because of the decisions that the women made. That would have been the greatest “Fashion Police” ever. But that’s really where it turned very serious and statement-oriented. The world has become so much more serious in the last 20 years. The social reckonings, the political landscape: The world is going to hell in a handbag. But let’s call it what it is. It’s a bunch of beautiful, talented, successful people, walking into a building to see if they won something. The consequence is, Does someone like your dress? And you’ll be the judge of that! Of course I will. One of the things people used to love was — as my mom used to say, when you sat on your couch at home, you didn’t say everybody looked wonderful. We were just giving voice to that. We tried to be the viewer. That’s why I’m saying: If you want to make a political statement, go to another position. Don’t stop. Because that is not my vibe. Let’s bring fun back. Are there any attendees whose style you tend to really like? Keri Russell always looks amazing. I’m going through, in my head, who the women are. Jean Smart always looks appropriate and yet glamorous. Who else do we have? Hannah Einbinder. Zendaya. Oh, forget it. Zendaya — okay, we’re all running for number two. It’s almost like, “Why bother?” Speaking of Jean Smart, though, I’m curious if her performance on “Hacks” ever called your mom to mind. Many people think Deborah Vance is based in part on Joan Rivers. Yes, of course. And my mother would be so happy that if there was anyone playing someone lightly based on her, that it was Jean Smart. She would be so happy. Not only is Jean so talented, but she is tall and elegant and blonde. My mother always joked that Cate Blanchett would play her in a movie. She got Jean Smart, which would thrill her to death. In the fifth season, an Emmy nominee this year, Deborah and her daughter D.J. have a real breakthrough in their relationship. Did you recognize this as true to life, or see yourself in Kaitlin Olson’s performance as D.J.? I actually haven’t watched it yet. I’ll sum it up: We leave the relationship in a really positive place overall. It’s really hard for me to watch these things. I can’t speak intelligently about it because I haven’t watched enough of the show for a multitude of reasons. When someone snuck me the pilot, I was not thrilled by how I was portrayed. But I do appreciate that there was an evolution of the relationship. Do I think where my character started was accurate? No. Do I love the fact that they portrayed evolution — which is a true theme between mothers and daughters? I love that. Speaking of mothers and daughters, have you ever re-watched the perennially viral clip of your mom and you walking out of “The Celebrity Apprentice” together after you were fired? Oh, God, no! I’m not sure if that was one of my greatest moments or one of my worst moments. Hell, no! I wonder what your mom would have made of the current landscape, where stars are more open about the work they’ve had done and Ozempic has redefined the red carpet. I think she would say, “Thank God — everybody’s caught up! And admitting it!” Back in the day, we would be looking behind people’s ears for fresh scars. Now, everyone’s like, “Look what I’ve done!” It’s clear you missed the red carpet, even as the prep is a bit stressful. What was it like walking away from awards-show reporting? We chose to walk away because… It’s like anything — you show up and you kind of don’t care. That was when my mom and I had the conversation. We both came to it separately that it was time to walk away. I was never planning on this. If you had asked me two weeks ago, “Would I ever go back?,” I would say no. And I still can’t believe I just said “Sure” without really thinking about it. I hate making this more serious than it is — I have a goal, which is to make it fun again. I’m going on my own personal campaign to bring fun back. title: ‘Back in Black’ Director on Lovable Serial Killer Doing “Bad Things for the Right Reasons” in Christopher Walken-Starrer
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 13, 2026 6:15am Back in Black Toronto Film Festival Back in Black , as a darkly funny crime drama, is no whodunnit. Ron Murphy’s satire about a failing funeral home has Christopher Walken starring as family patriarch Clyde Mortimer who is staring down bankruptcy. But his business enjoys a sudden rebound in fortune when Sam, his quiet granddaughter played by Ella Ballentine, triggers a suspicious rise in the number of small-town murders that leaves local police stumped and a trail of cadavers arriving on his doorstep. All of which begs the question: what is it about benevolent serial killers that’s expected to have Toronto Film Festival audiences cheering Sam on as an antihero while her town’s local kill count rises? “It’s a bit of a trick, isn’t it? Most people in test screenings that we’ve done are rooting for (Sam). And meanwhile, what she’s doing is morally reprehensible,” Murphy tells The Hollywood Reporter ahead of Back in Black , his debut feature, having a world premiere at TIFF. Related Stories Movies Fina Strazza to Star in, Produce Romantic Drama 'Any Way You Want Me' (Exclusive) Movies Toronto: Irene Dionisio's 'IDDA' Lands at FilmClub Distribuzione for Italy (Exclusive) It turns out Sam, an embalmer by day and cold-blooded killer by night, is preying on local townsfolk because she doesn’t want to see Mortimer and his wife, played by Jane Curtin, fight over finances and be denied a dignified retirement. “I’m asking the audience, how far would you be willing to go for someone you love,” Murphy adds about his morality-bending psychological drama that has Fargo meets Six Feet Under vibes. Not that Walken’s Mortimer character, for his devotion to his family and its generational business, isn’t himself cunning and ruthless. Murphy recalls getting on the phone with the Hollywood legend with his prolific film resume and Oscar-winning role in 1978’s The Deer Hunter soon after he read his Back in Black script. “I think he was testing me because he said, ‘Ron, I’ve played these dark characters for 50 years, these morally questionable characters,’” and Walken was suggesting that, at his age, actors just want to play normal people. After insisting Clyde Mortimer was not a bad man, but in service to people he loved during tough times, Murphy added with an Avis, Try Harder sales pitch: “By the way, I didn’t write this for you. Nick (Torokvei) and I wrote it for Jack Lemmon. And he’s not available. You’re our second choice.” Murphy is also with the layers of moral contradictions in Back in Black , urging audiences to explore how, in a world filled with injustice and inequity, serial killers can help as well as harm — even if that helps Mortimer cash in on bereaved relatives by upselling them on pricey caskets. “It’s important that a bad person gets their comeuppance. But if they’re doing bad things for the right reasons, then an audience’s morality bends, as we’ve seen in the screenings. That’s very upside down, because innocent people are being harmed,” the director argues. For Murphy, while Back in Black is his first feature, he has deep roots in the TV business. He began as an assistant to the late John Candy, and from there directed episodic comedies that starred Steve Carell, Leslie Neilson, Tim Conway, Snoop Dogg, and even Michael Cera and Drake in early small screen roles. His Canadian TV directing credits include Trailer Park Boys, Heartland, Lost Girl and Wynonna Earp. But with his first feature, Murphy has looked to offer, via satire, his own take on our wider economy and politics. “There’s definitely a sort of darkness in the culture that we all feel, certainly since the pandemic. And it’s disorienting, and I feel I want to reflect that darkness in a comic way,” he explains. Another anomaly in Back in Black is Sam, as played by Ballentine, a child actor graduating to adult roles, has no lines to speak as she and her grandfather quietly share a language of love and loyalty. “In film school, I was obsessed with Buster Keaton, and I’ve always wanted to make a silent film. I just think there’s an elegance to telling a story with no words,” Murphy says. Having made his first feature long after he left film school, Murphy adds he’s looking forward to connecting, with his TIFF world premiere, to a theatrical audience after long working on TV sets and in edit rooms where viewers are well out of sight. But as to how Toronto audiences greet Back in Black , whether with laughter, gasps or silence, Murphy has no expectations to avoid opening night distress: “I’ve learned during my television career to be very Buddhist about the material and to abandon your attachment to outcomes. If you think it’s going to be funny and they don’t laugh, your heart is broken. Or you’re surprised they laugh at something else you didn’t think was funny.” Instead, Murphy is looking to Toronto for fresh eyes for a movie he and his team have long been working on. “As soon as it screens at TIFF, it belongs to the audience, and they can do with it whatever they want, respond to it however they want, and I’m really good at just letting go,” he adds. THR

title: ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Gets Modern War-Zone Update From Lakeem Rose (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Sep 13, 2026 6:15am PT ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Gets Modern War-Zone Update From Lakeem Rose (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Cannes Prize-Winning Nepal Oscar Entry ‘Elephants in the Fog’ Sells Wide for Best Friend Forever (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Trans Pregnancy Drama ‘Aman’ Boards Parallax Films for Global Sales Ahead of Toronto and London Premieres (EXCLUSIVE) 5 hours ago Inside ‘Ah Girl,’ the Singapore Drama Built From a Director’s Own Childhood: ‘We Can’t Fly Without First Learning How to Walk’ 20 hours ago See All Fast Motion Films British writer-director Lakeem Rose, is developing his feature debut, a contemporary adaptation of William Shakespeare’s “ Much Ado About Nothing ,” with Canadian producers Plato Fountidakis and Paul Rapovski and Hong Kong-based producer and casting director Mike Leeder. In Rose’s version, the story shifts to a world just after a modern-day war, centering on four returning soldiers who reunite at the house of a family friend. Old grudges resurface alongside fresh romantic entanglements and a scheme that threatens to unravel everyone involved. Related Stories 'Alpha Gang’ Review: Cate Blanchett, Chris Pine and an All-Star Cast Play Space Aliens in David and Nathan Zellner’s Endearingly Goofy Sci-Fi Spoof ‘A Common Story’ Review: A Stunningly Played Study of a Couple Whose Inability to Articulate Their Emotions Drives Them Apart The dialogue stays true to Shakespeare’s Early Modern English, paired with subtitles in contemporary English, even as the setting and visual world around the text are reconstructed for today’s viewers. Rose is also folding sequences styled after silent cinema into the modern-day military backdrop. Popular on Variety “As always, we have to edit these texts to flow as a screenplay. I’ve been studying how filmmakers and performers like Kenneth Branagh and David Harewood bring this language to life,” said Rose. “The language has survived for 400 years for a reason. Our experiment is to change the context around it and see what happens when these characters, relationships and ideas are placed in a world that feels immediate to people now.” Fountidakis is producing, with both he and Rapovski steering the project in their roles as managing partners at Fast Motion Films; Clever Creature handles the film’s international sales and distribution. Between them, the two Canadian producers have spent decades working in genre film and television, having contributed to “Enhanced,” “Believer,” “Mutant X,” “Bullet Proof Monk,” “The Chronicles of Riddick,” “Scott Pilgrim vs. the World” and “Lost Girl.” That background in action design and production is expected to inform the look of the film’s military setting, from its locations to its physical action sequences. “Independent cinema depends on backing new voices with bold tastes,” said Fountidakis. “This modern adaptation has the opportunity to introduce Shakespeare to audiences who might never otherwise engage with his work. Lakeem has a distinctive perspective on the material, and the combination of Shakespearean language, contemporary genre filmmaking and a post-conflict setting gives the project a very fresh identity.” Red Packet Media’s Leeder rounds out the producing team. He has been based in Hong Kong since 1990 and has built his career around Asian and international genre titles, having worked on “Rogue One: A Star Wars Story,” Jet Li’s “Fearless,” “Man of Tai Chi,” the “Ip Man” franchise and “The Raid” films. “What interests me is the collision of traditions,” said Leeder. “The language remains Shakespeare’s, but the world around it belongs to contemporary genre cinema. Setting ‘Much Ado’ in the aftermath of such immediate conflict gives the romance, humor and deception a new tone, while the silent visual passages allow parts of the story to be told entirely through image. Plato’s genre experience and Lakeem’s background in theatre and music make this a genuinely unusual way into the material.” Rose’s path into filmmaking began with an English degree at the University of Oxford, where he appeared in a staging of Shakespeare’s “Love’s Labour’s Lost” under the guidance of Shakespeare scholar Jonathan Bate. His work outside narrative film spans music, visual media and documentary projects. A separate documentary series, “Reinventing Shakespeare,” is tracking the film’s progress, following Rose and his collaborators as they work through what Shakespeare’s writing can offer a new generation of viewers. Rose and Fountidakis plan to take meetings around the project at the Toronto Film Festival market. The adaptation is in development now, with a 2027 release targeted. title: Fina Strazza to Star in, Produce Romantic Drama ‘Any Way You Want Me’ (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 13, 2026 6:05am Fina Strazza, Rana Strazza Hunter Abrams Fina Strazza, the Fear Street: Prom Queen and Paper Girls star, is set to produce and star in the romantic drama Any Way You Want Me, directed by Rana Strazza, who is also her mother. Strazza will play Billie Blake, who returns home when her mother inherits a dress shop next to her high school sweetheart Calvin Wilkes’ diner. Forced to face Calvin, Billie must contend with the truth, and lies, that ended their romance, according to a synopsis from the producers. Strazza joins an ensemble cast that includes Cobie Smulders, Iris Apatow, Brian Altemus and Callan Potter. Anyway You Want Me , set in 1950s New England and now shooting in Toronto, is also being shopped this week to international buyers at TIFF : The Market. Related Stories Movies Toronto: Irene Dionisio's 'IDDA' Lands at FilmClub Distribuzione for Italy (Exclusive) Movies 'Words Are Weapons': Michaël R. Roskam on Turning a WWII Fake-Newspaper Prank Into a Heist Movie “My mother has been my greatest collaborator for my entire career. She is the smartest, most hardworking woman I have ever met. There are few folks better equipped to create the equally enchanting and sentimentally accurate world she’s built. To be producing alongside her and portraying our beautiful Billie Blake in her love letter to the films that influenced her own artistry is such a full-circle joy,” Fina Strazza said in a statement on Sunday. The film will be produced by First Magnitude Films and Stagg Forrest Films, with Matt Strazza, writer/director Rana Strazza, and Jeff Cryder serving as executive producers. Myrthin Stagg and Kate Forrest also share producer credits. “As new and older generations revisit analog charms and long for ordinary connection in a hyper-connected world, Any Way You Want Me is a simple love story crafted to emulate the movies of a bygone era,” Rana Strazza added in her own statement. Fina Strazza is represented by Paradigm and Mara Entertainment. Cobie Smulders is represented by UTA, while Brian Altemus is represented by Innovative Artists and Linden Entertainment. Callan Potter is represented by The Talent House and David Dean Management. Iris Apatow is represented by UTA and 3 Arts Entertainment. THR

title: Toronto: Irene Dionisio’s ‘IDDA’ Lands at FilmClub Distribuzione for Italy (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 13, 2026 5:31am IDDA Toronto Film Festival FilmClub Distribuzione has acquired Irene Dionisio’s IDDA Mount Etna drama for Italy after a world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival as part of the Platform program. The deal with Rai Cinema International Distribution is for Dionisio’s second narrative feature that stars Tecla Insolia and Romana Maggiora Vergano and is being shopped at TIFF: The Market in Toronto. IDDA follows childhood friends Adele and Sofia, now in their thirties, whose lifelong bond is challenged during a journey through the volcanic landscapes of Sicily’s Mount Etna. Related Stories Movies 'Words Are Weapons': Michaël R. Roskam on Turning a WWII Fake-Newspaper Prank Into a Heist Movie Movies Inside 'NAZA,' the Bombshell Exposé on IDF's War in Gaza Andrea Curti, CEO and head of acquisitions at FilmClub Distribuzione, a Minerva Pictures’ company, in a statement on Sunday said: “We’re extremely proud to have the chance to bring one of the most awaited titles of the season to the Italian audience. IDDA is first and foremost an amazing journey with wonderful people: Irene Dionisio, Giovanni Pompili and the whole production team, and the amazing cast with three of the most talented voices of our contemporary cinema.” Dionisio made documentaries before moving into narrative filmmaking with Pawn Street, which debuted at Venice in 2017. She co-wrote IDDA with Marco Borromei ( Small Body ). “I’m especially happy that the film is now beginning its journey toward audiences through such an important distribution release. I hope IDDA can reach viewers in Italy and internationally, opening a space for dialogue about friendship, change, belonging and the difficult transitions we all experience. I’m thrilled to share the film with audiences and grateful to everyone helping it find its way into cinemas and homes around the world,” Dionisio said in her own statement. The distribution deal was negotiated by Fulvio Firrito for Rai Cinema International Distribution, which is handling international sales on the film, and Andrea Curti for FilmClub Distribuzione. IDDA is produced by Giovanni Pompili, Isabella Weber, Filippo Montalto, Francesco Montalto, Francesco Grisi, Giorgia Priolo and Antonio Miyakawa. THR

title: Variety and Chanel’s Women in Film Bash: Ayo Edebiri, Lily-Rose Depp, Michelle Yeoh, Courteney Cox and More Light Up TIFF
full_text: POUPAY JUTHARAT / CHANEL Variety and Chanel ‘s annual Women in Film dinner was the place to see and be chic at the Toronto Film Festival on Friday night. The hottest invite of the festival gathered prominent women and nonbinary filmmakers, where the legendary fashion house co-hosted an evening to remember with Variety co-presidents Ramin Setoodeh (also co-editor-in-chief) and Dea Lawrence. When Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh entered the bar for the evening cocktail hour, Emmy winners Sarah Paulson and Colman Domingo greeted her with hugs. Soon, Patricia Arquette breezed in, pulling in her fellow Oscar winner for a quick photo. Related Stories 'Burgundy' Review: An Attractive, Light-Bodied Wine Doc With a Good Nose but No Legs 'Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing' Review: A Handsome Ode to an Oft-Disrespected Sport That power quartet — plus Chanel ambassadors and actresses Ayo Edebiri and Lily-Rose Depp, Noomi Rapace, Luke Evans, David Harbour, India Amarteifio, Rosalind Eleazar, Cole Sprouse, Amber Midthunder, Jessica Henwick, Charlie Heaton, “I Play Rocky” breakout Anthony Ippolito , Cooper Raiff, Mariana di Girolamo, Emanuela Postacchini, Mackenzie Davis and more — epitomized the top-tier talent who assembled to celebrate the achievements of women and nonbinary filmmakers in this year’s lineup. Popular on Variety While the term “filmmaker” generally refers to directors, the event saluted many powerful multihyphenates, like actor-director Fala Chen (“Bloodline”) or Courteney Cox, who launched her directorial debut “Evil Genius” out of the fest. “At Variety , we’ve made a commitment to cover parity in the entertainment industry and the importance of female representation on the big screen. And while there have been significant strides, there’s still much room for improvement,” said Setoodeh, kicking off the event. While Hollywood is having a banner year at the movies, Setoodeh noted, none of the top 15 films at the box office were solely directed by women. “That’s why this dinner is so important. It’s an opportunity for you all to network, to come together, to brainstorm,” he said, asking the female filmmakers and producers in the crowd to raise their hands high. “If you’re an executive, here’s who you need to talk to.” Lawrence drove that point home, quoting the late Gloria Steinem: “Representation is not just who gets to appear in the story. It’s about who gets to tell the story. And so tonight we celebrate the women who are doing exactly that: creating, directing, writing, producing, and leading the way, opening those doors for the next generation of women.” Sarah Paulson, Michelle Yeoh and Colman Domingo POUPAY JUTHARAT Ayo Edebiri POUPAY JUTHARAT Chung Suet Ying and Fala Chen POUPAY JUTHARAT Luke Evans POUPAY JUTHARAT Seth Rogen and Lauren Miller Rogen POUPAY JUTHARAT This year’s TIFF lineup proves progress is possible, as 35% of the official selection is directed or co-directed by women, like “Love of Your Life” from Rachel Morrison or “Josephine” by Beth de Araújo. That impressive figure — a goal that TIFF leadership set for 2028, but reached two years early — is made possible when organizations like Chanel and publications like Variety hold Hollywood’s decision-makers to account, said TIFF’s Chief Business and Marketing Officer Jennifer Frees. “Chanel and Variety share TIFF’s passion for supporting the remarkable creators who continue to shape the future of culture and of cinema,” Frees said. “So with that in mind, this evening is a celebration of world-class creativity and the community that it fosters.” One such initiative is the Chanel Women Creators’ Network, an extension of the TIFF Share Her Journey’s annual Writers’ Lab. “At Chanel, it’s nothing new for us to support women — because our founder was a woman,” said Gregoire Collignon, president of Chanel Canada, referring to Coco Chanel. “Since the ’30s, she was designing and supporting women in film.” This program, established in 2020, continues that legacy, he added, and “reinforces the house’s commitment to championing women in the arts and to creating opportunities for their artistic and personal development.” Carol Nguyen is a 2025 fellow whose documentary “Still Night, Burning House” is also debuting at this year’s fest. The 2026 fellows are Shannon Walsh, Hannah Vastinsalo, Shannon Welby and Amelia Eloisa. “These four exceptional creators represent the vision, the originality and the artistic excellence that define the next generation of filmmaking,” Frees said. “Through their work, they’re expanding perspectives, they’re challenging conventions, and they’re reminding us why diverse stories matter so much.” After the speeches, the mingling continued: “Being Heumann” director Sîan Heder and star Ruth Madeley fielded congratulations for how well their film played as the festival’s opening night selection. Next to them, Lauren Miller Rogen (“Babies”) and Seth Rogen chatted with Ziwe Fumudoh. When the party moved upstairs for an intimate, seated dinner, Rogen’s signature laugh rang out above the din of conversation and the clanking of forks and knives. This fashionable crowd was ready to let their hair down and have some fun amid the business of the fest. title: ‘The Stunt Driver’ Review: Jay Baruchel Takes a Leap into Tepid Biopic Territory
full_text: Sep 13, 2026 5:12am PT ‘The Stunt Driver’ Review: Jay Baruchel Takes a Leap into Tepid Biopic Territory Baruchel takes the lead for a period comedy about a hapless stunt driver that isn’t as funny as the documentary it’s based on. By Vadim Rizov Plus Icon Vadim Rizov Latest ‘Le Faux Soir’ Review: Fake News Tells the Truth in an Earnest, Slow-Paced Period Piece 2 days ago ‘The Sun Never Sets’ Review: Dakota Fanning and Jake Johnson Split, Maybe, in Joe Swanberg’s Unsatisfying Romcom 2 weeks ago Many Tarantino projects never happened 17 years ago See All Jay Baruchel in "The Stunt Driver," courtesy Film Cardinal In “ The Stunt Driver ,” Jay Baruchel reteams with his “Goon” director Michael Dowse and takes on a showy lead part as stunt driver Ken Carter, who’s best remembered for a jump he didn’t make: a proposed mile-long leap over the St. Lawrence River in a rocket-powered car. The five years spent on that ill-fated project were captured in the 1981 documentary “The Devil At Your Heels,” which “The Stunt Driver” credits as source material but doesn’t improve on. While the technical aspects of the period recreation are impressive, this remake never finds its own reason to exist. Related Stories 'Bunker' Review: Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz Are Brilliant in Florian Zeller's Riveting, Slightly Overstated Thriller of Isolation and Invasion 'Snowfall' Spinoff 'The Drop' Is an Evocative, If Uneven, Portrait of South L.A. in the Gangsta Rap Era: TV Review As in the doc, Carter is introduced executing a stunt jump which leaves him injured and begging the crowd not to leave, addressing them from the stretcher before being carried off. That naked lust for the adulation generated by danger is more bluntly stated when Carter repeats variations on “I gotta jump, people like me” as sufficient justification for his extremely dangerous stunt, the requirements of which include constructing a 90-foot ramp to launch the car. The documentary’s archival footage is seamlessly intercut with staged recreations as Carter assembles a small team of enablers: engineer Dick Keller (Ed Helms), sports agent Bill Wilkins (Dan Bakkedahl), goofy Quebecois protege and hype-man Danny Lafortune (Marc Beaupré). In standard biopic fashion, Ken’s wife Gloria (Laurence Lebouef) is relegated to worrying and suffering in the background. Popular on Variety Granted interviews with surviving friends and access to unused footage from the documentary, Dowse takes particular advantage of a forgotten radio interview in which Carter was hypnotized. While the additional insight from this rediscovered artifact provides the foundation for a degree of vulnerability and self-revelation that the documentary couldn’t tap into, Carter’s fears remains one-note even when grounded in reality. Carter’s naked craving to be liked and the class-based chip on his shoulder take on sinister connotations at moments when Baruchel sounds strangely like Richard Nixon, further muddying the emotional waters. When not mired in pathos, Baruchel plays Carter as an eccentric showboater, especially in his elaborate dialogue, which is far beyond the quotable but comparatively low-key man shown in the documentary; the final scene’s slow dissolve fade from Baruchel to the real subject only heighten the oddities of the actor’s performance. Speaking to the trade-war tensions of the present moment, “The Stunt Driver” also makes Carter a zealous Canadian patriot who derides rival stuntman Evel Knievel (Ben Foster) as an unwelcome “yankee doodle dandy” and later yells, “I eat Americans like you for breakfast!” Besides the additional psychologizing and final 20 minutes, which address Carter’s years after the jump, the film makes one major alteration to the source text. Presumably because the name of the American stunt driver who took Carter’s place on the jump, Kenny Powers (as in the protagonist of “Eastbound & Down”), would be a distraction for many viewers, both name and personality have been changed to Quebecois comic relief Lafontaine. While both the casting and location choices honor Kane and Baruchel’s shared Quebec background, the change of Powers’ nationality omits another logical place to heighten the anti-American angle. (In a very specific feat, the film’s most notable performance is arguably given by Joe Coben as “Devil” director Bob Fortier; the actor’s speech patterns are eerily like the real ‘70s thing to a degree unheard since Jon Voight channeled Howard Cosell in “Ali.”) The first 80 minutes toggle between restaging scenes from the documentary while matching its academy ratio, and alternately providing additional context in widescreen, with a third aspect ratio thrown into the mix at the climax. The idea is clear: the documentary shows some but not all of the truth, so the new film is supplemented by a glossier but more emotionally truthful format and complemented at the end by a new format to heighten Carter’s anxiety. DP Sara Mishara does a bravura job of using numerous formats (digital and actual 16mm, as well as 35mm stock, among others) and rendering them period-plausible as well as handsomely lit and colored in their own right. “The Stunt Driver” is, nonetheless, slow going, and less enjoyable than the funnier, springier documentary it takes great pains to expand on. ‘The Stunt Driver’ Review: Jay Baruchel Takes a Leap into Tepid Biopic Territory Reviewed at Toronto Film Festival (Special Presentations), Sept. 11, 2026. title: ‘Words Are Weapons’: Michaël R. Roskam on Turning a WWII Fake-Newspaper Prank Into a Heist Movie
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 13, 2026 5:00am 'Le Faux Soir' Frakas-Productions-Rectangle-Productions-_-Goodfellas-RTL-Belgium In November 1943, a group of Belgian journalists and printers pulled off one of the great stunts of the occupation: they intercepted the Nazi-controlled newspaper Le Soir (The Evening) and replaced it with a satirical counterfeit, Le Faux Soir (The Fake Evening), mocking the occupiers. It was the world’s first media hack. In his film version, Belgian director Michaël R. Roskam ( Bullhead , The Drop , Racer and the Jailbird ) tells the story as a caper — “ Ocean’s Eleven , but with a newspaper” — featuring a cast of Belgium and France’s funniest actors. Le Faux Soir has its world premiere at TIFF and is being sold by Goodfellas worldwide. Related Stories Movies Inside 'NAZA,' the Bombshell Exposé on IDF's War in Gaza TIFF RISING STAR 'Happily Ever After' Star Shuhua Yeh Makes the Leap From K-pop Idol to Actress: "It's Really Happening" Roskam spoke to THR from Brussels about researching 1940s jokes and linotype machines, why authoritarians can’t stand being laughed at, and the limits of satire. When did you first hear about Le Faux Soir , and how did you decide to make a film about it? That’s actually my co-writer, Bernard Falaise. He’s about my age, and he decided that he wanted to do film studies, so he went back to university. At some point, he had this course about piracy in media and satire. In that course, they had been talking about Le Faux Soir. All of a sudden, their phones started buzzing — the ones who had them still active got notifications — it was the attacks in Paris, on [French satire magazine] Charlie Hebdo. A year later they had a choice: either write a thesis or write a script. He wanted to write a script on the Le Faux Soir story. He came to me because we’re friends and he really helped me with casting on Bullhead . He’s French-speaking, I’m Flemish-speaking. He’s like, “Dude, I want to make the script. It’s tough. You want to give it a read?” And he told me the story, and I was like, “That’s a movie. This is amazing. I’ve never heard of it.” No one on the Flemish side [of Belgium], with very few exceptions, had ever heard of this story. Even on the French-speaking side, it was mostly the subscribers of Le Soir , because every year they do a kind of article about it. I’m like, “Dude, if you manage to write this, I’ll direct it.” So he tried, and his script was fairly cool. But I said, “You already told me the story, and I see images, how I would direct it, and your script is not what I see.” But I wouldn’t want to steal the project from him so I said “Let’s write it together, and I’ll direct it.” Michaël R. Roskam talking with actors on the set of ‘Le Faux Soir’ Maxence-Dedry What was the hardest thing about cracking the script? The hardest problem was the text [of the fake newspaper] because the text is funny. It’s a satire. The text is funny, but the text is also old, it’s from the ’40s. A few of the jokes still hold up, but a lot of them refer to people or things where it’s more “I feel it’s funny, but I don’t get the joke, because I don’t know what they’re talking about.” And I was way more fascinated in how they pulled the thing off. Because writing a satire isn’t the dangerous bit, it’s publishing it. How they did it felt to me like a heist movie. Ocean’s Eleven , but with a newspaper. That’s what I said: we need to be very disciplined about the humor, to make it funny without making a satire movie, like Life is Beautiful — which is fantastic — or Taika Waititi’s Jojo Rabbit . I didn’t want to make a satire. I wanted to make a realistic movie about very realistic, very funny people risking their lives. How did that shape the casting? Even at the script stage, I said: “Dude, we need to cast people with funny bones.” I needed François Damiens, I needed Arieh Worthalter, I needed Bouli Lanners. They’re big names in the French-speaking community, the funniest guys on the planet. Bouli is funny and poetic. Arieh is a great, sensitive and funny actor. François Damiens is a funny clown who does everything to hide that he’s actually a fantastic actor. And then you have Mélanie Thierry, who is very poetic, serious, but she also has a little something, a twinkle in the eye. When I had my Ocean’s Eleven together, it was also about holding them back, or they’d turn the film into a full-blown comedy. What’s compelling is that the heroes here aren’t the typical resistance fighters planting bombs. They’re people making jokes, puns and silly poems as a way to resist fascism. I see this film as right in between something like Chaplin’s The Great Dictator and Inglourious Basterds. For me, it was not about doing what Chaplin does, making that kind of satire. It was about showing how Chaplin does it. Michaël R. Roskam holds up a copy of the fake ‘Le Soir’ Guillaume-Van-Laethem I’m a print guy, so I was geeking out on the mechanics — where they get the paper, the presses, how they copy it. How deep did you go into the research? My way of working is to learn everything about the subject I’m making a movie on. From Bullhead , I still know how to raise cattle and bring them to the meat market, illegally and legally. I know the holdups I staged in Racer and the Jailbird would work in real life. Here, I know how to print a newspaper using 1940s technology. I could be a project manager of a newspaper in the ’40s. I went to museums and started finding people, retired people in their 80s and 90s, who told me how it was. Then younger people who learned from the older people, who are rediscovering the old techniques. La Démocrate in France is a museum, but they still print a newspaper, La Démocrate, using the old methods. And they’re young guys. It’s so amazing. Discovering the linotype was one of the most magical things I have ever encountered in my career. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a machine I didn’t know existed that is still alive only because of the passion of people keeping it alive. It’s literally a wonder. I still get goosebumps when I see it. I can look at it for hours. Just the sound of it. For your readers: the linotype is a machine that automates typing, where the letters are melted into a mold, instead of setting every letter by hand. It’s an automatic process, but still mechanical. It’s nothing digital. When I saw this, I knew: this is what we need. We need to evoke those moments. There’s something about the physicality of it. If you were doing a story about social media satire today, visually you’d just have people looking at their phones. Some little text appearing on screen, yeah. What does this story have to say to audiences at this moment? Well, the reason why we tell historical movies is always in the now, in the moment when you decide that the story is important. It came to Bernard at one of the craziest, most horrific events of the last 10 years: the shooting at the Charlie Hebdo editorial offices. This act of terrorism against satire. And because of the issue of fake news. Fighting fake news today is dangerous, but during the Second World War, you could get a bullet in your head for making the wrong comment, the wrong joke. I hope that young people will watch this film with their grandparents, and see that there have always been people fighting against fake news, against how the truth has been bent throughout history. It was done with weapons and violence, but very often it was also done with words. One of our characters says: “Why do the Nazis burn books? Because words are weapons.” And he means it. It’s always been like that with satire. It’s like making fun of the king. It’s forbidden, but it’s the only way you can hurt him. That’s what I wanted to do. Although it’s almost ironic that today, so much of the spoofing is coming from authoritarian regimes. Russia famously has farms that copy Le Monde or Der Spiegel — the exact websites — and promote their own fake news within them. They’re doing exactly what Le Faux Soir did, but for the opposite purpose. Exactly. Isn’t that ironic? If an alien were to look from space at the modern day, he might think that we, the establishment, are the Nazis of the time, and that the ones on the right hacking us are the resistance of the ’40s. We’re defending democracy, but there are some people who are victims of that situation, and they want this system to be dismantled, and they’re using everything they can. I believe that I’m fighting for the right thing. I’m for democracy. But I don’t know. Maybe I’m on the wrong side. I don’t know. It’s a terrible thought to think that I’m on the wrong side, man. It also raises the question of how effective satire really is against authoritarianism. Those famous Berlin cabaret artists who mocked Hitler were all either shot or exiled. Le Faux Soir doesn’t topple the Nazis either. The satirists are rounded up and shot. Satire is not like blowing up a bridge. But if it works, if you can make it work, you can plant the seeds in the heads of the people. It has a toppling effect. Satire has a mental effect. It is the first button of the emperor’s clothes being opened, and then the next one. And if you continue doing it, at some point he’s naked on his throne and everybody’s laughing, and that’s when he loses. That’s why authoritarian regimes hate satire. They can’t stand it. They come back with falsification, with fake news, which is not the same as satire. This interview has been edited for length and clarity THR

title: ‘Girl Group’ Review: Rebel Wilson’s Bawdy Pop Comedy Is All Fizz and Little Substance
full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:52am PT ‘Girl Group’ Review: Rebel Wilson’s Bawdy Pop Comedy Is All Fizz and Little Substance Wilson stars as a coach to a crew of singing misfits whose harmony as an ensemble is the movie’s greatest asset. By Natalia Winkelman Plus Icon Natalia Winkelman Latest ‘By Any Means’ Review: Mark Wahlberg Teaches the Virtues of Violence in Elegance Bratton’s Bluntly Drawn Historical Thriller 1 week ago ‘The Accompanist’ Review: Susan Sarandon Shines as a Problematic Foster Parent in Zach Woods’ Unsteady Directorial Debut 3 months ago ‘The Breadwinner’ Review: Nate Bargatze Bumbles Through a Domestic Comedy That Thinks Incompetent Dads are Still Funny 4 months ago See All TIFF Toward the end of Rebel Wilson ’s “ Girl Group ,” a fizzy, gaudy clone of “Pitch Perfect” sculpted from the mentor formula of “Bad News Bears,” the movie spirals into an interminable sequence of pop music performances. The song-and-dance numbers are so awkwardly endless that they call to mind the denouement of a very different pop spectacle: Brady Corbet’s “Vox Lux,” in which Natalie Portman’s megastar becomes a tragic emblem of the emptiness of the celebrity industrial complex. Related Stories ‘The Stunt Driver’ Review: Jay Baruchel Takes a Leap into Tepid Biopic Territory 'Practical Magic 2' Review: Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman Don't Quite Cast a Spell in an Overlong, Predictable Sequel “Girl Group,” which follows a band of misfits competing to become signed music artists, could not be further removed from that type of cynicism if it were set on a different planet, and Wilson, starring as the group’s coach, seems hardly to know the meaning of the word. A comedy whiz who became famous for playing — as she wrote in her memoir — “the fat funny girl,” Wilson has little on her mind here beyond sparkly merriment, and “Girl Group” is an accordingly flamboyant extravaganza designed to have audiences humming and nodding along without thinking a single thought. Popular on Variety There are occasions that call for this sort of broadly comforting trifle, on airplanes or in late-night popcorn sessions. “Girl Group” seems even to nod to its position on the feel-good shelf when, after a trying day, a character suggests to her sister that they head home to snuggle and rent “Pitch Perfect.” This movie — despite performances from a veritable diva corps d’elite, including Nicole Scherzinger and Ashley Roberts of The Pussycat Dolls, the Spice Girls’ Mel C, and All Saints’ Shaznay Lewis — never reaches the emotional heights of that rewatch-ready franchise, nor does it really strive to. It’s instead at ease as a second-stringer, a congenial romp that exists only as it unspools before you, then dissipates like stage fog the moment it’s over. The story opens in 1997, as five friends at a London girls’ school prepare to perform in their auditorium. Backstage, a member of the crew frets to her teacher (a brief but keen Sally Hawkins) about the pressure, before the pals — who perform under the name Gurlfriends — head onstage and bring the house down. The overture gives way to a whirlwind montage of the group’s ascent, culminating with a member named Tassie (played in the present day by Wilson) ditching the gang to try and make it as a solo act. The effort fails, and Tassie sinks into an alcoholic stupor from which she emerges, years later, to find that she’s been replaced for the reunion tour by a warbling prima donna. This is where the real story starts, and where Wilson might have been better off centering the movie all along. Sentenced to community service at a youth center, Tassie meets a group of Gen Z-ers whom she’s assigned to mentor ahead of an upcoming competition. The washed-up star sees their talent as a chance to rehabilitate her own image, but the peppy, ambitious teens have aspirations of their own, and as Tassie sets about molding them into a glossy vision of millennial pop stardom, her narcissism increasingly becomes a liability to their success. There are feeble gestures at a generational divide over female sexuality and pop-star image, as when one of the younger crew exclaims that Gurlfriends were “totally playing into the male gaze.” But such moments are so few and far between that it feels as if Wilson forgot about the theme halfway through, or, more likely, found it too thorny to properly unpack. Fair enough: prickly questions about how famous women can or should display themselves are unlikely to be settled by a broad comedy more interested in cramming in mile-a-minute jokes. Much of the film’s humor consists of bawdy clowning, with a handful of contemporary reference-laden jokes thrown in for good measure. And despite Wilson’s frank discussions of weight and weight loss in her memoir, there’s a curious abundance of size-related gags. At one point, a child accuses Tassie of looking like she “ate” Sabrina Carpenter. Elsewhere, Jennifer Coolidge, gamely playing Gurlfriends’ manager, encourages Tassie to promote Splurt, a nutrition bar with a laxative effect. Its potential to induce sudden bowel urgency in front of a crowd does not go unnoticed. Amid the slew of tired gags, the harmony among the younger cast is the film’s greatest asset, and their easy rapport and naturalism help cut against the run-of-the-mill story. The standouts are Chabely Ponce, as an acoustic guitar-slinging crooner, and Lilah Pate, who excels as the group’s leader, despite having to suffer through one ill-conceived scene involving an aggressive, nonconsensual kiss. Their enthusiasm as an ensemble suggests a warmer movie, one in which the nonconformists take center stage as they blossom into more confident versions of themselves. But lost in the surrounding muddle and often eclipsed by Wilson’s relentless mugging, their stories wind up playing second fiddle. Their vivacity may be enough to break through Tassie’s vanity, but it can’t wholly elevate the movie around them. ‘Girl Group’ Review: Rebel Wilson’s Bawdy Pop Comedy Is All Fizz and Little Substance Reviewed at Toronto Film Festival (Gala Presentations), Sept. 11, 2026. title: Tom Nicoll Looks Beyond Male Influencer Culture in TIFF Title ‘Salvation’: ‘I Don’t Think Anyone’s Ever Been Insulted Into Changing Their Mind’
full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:24am PT Tom Nicoll Looks Beyond Male Influencer Culture in TIFF Title ‘Salvation’: ‘I Don’t Think Anyone’s Ever Been Insulted Into Changing Their Mind’ By Callum McLennan Plus Icon Callum McLennan Latest ‘I Don’t Know’: Kenneth Branagh on Directing, ‘Harry Potter’ and How Christopher Nolan Had Him Speaking Russian Backwards 4 weeks ago Director Frieda Luk on Olivia Luccardi’s ‘Sacred Creatures’ Role and the Fine Line Between ‘Crazy’ and ‘Enlightened’ 4 weeks ago ‘How the F— Would You Get This Movie Made in America?’ Christine Vachon, Film4, BBC Film Put ‘Trainspotting,’ ‘Ratcatcher’ and ‘The Wicker Man’ Through the 2026 Greenlight Test 4 weeks ago See All Liam Harkins as Danny in Salvation Scottish writer-director Tom Nicoll is unveling at Toronto his buzzy debut “Salvation.” It tracks an aspiring online life coach whose attempt to reinvent himself and then sell that transformation to others pulls him in increasingly desperate directions. The psychological and blackly comic thriller world premieres in TIFF ’s Discovery section, having already been selected for the BFI and British Council’s Great 8 showcase at Cannes. MetFilm Sales recently boarded world sales on the film, which stars Liam Harkins, Stephen McMillan, Kathleen McDermott and Conor McCarron. Related Stories 'Snowfall' Spinoff 'The Drop' Is an Evocative, If Uneven, Portrait of South L.A. in the Gangsta Rap Era: TV Review ‘Back to Buenos Aires’ Review: Marco Bechis’ Return to the Screen Covers Similar Ground to Earlier Works but is Only Fitfully Effective Set largely in Greenock, a post-industrial Scottish town, “Salvation” follows Danny Carlton, played by Harkins, as he emerges from a self-improvement retreat convinced he has found the way forward. Having been transformed, at least in his own mind, by charismatic guru Marshall Allison (Kevin O’Loughlin), Danny sets off to build a life coaching business of his own. The problem is that virtually nobody wants what he is selling while the money he has spent and borrowed pursuing it grows. Popular on Variety For Nicoll, the film was never primarily about finding easy targets in the world of male influencers. “I suppose, in general, in my life, I’m interested in that idea of what people find purpose in, what people choose to do with their lives, what they find value in, what they choose to put their energy into,” he told Variety . With Danny, that became a question of “what is lacking” to compel someone’s move towards a culture offering answers, status and self-optimization. “I don’t think anyone’s ever been insulted into changing their mind,” Nicoll explained. “It’s easy to point and laugh at someone.” A sweeping satire of the influencer sphere might provide “easy jokes” for five or ten minutes, he argues, but understanding why somebody is susceptible is the harder and more interesting motivation to pursue. We see Danny’s excitement and defence of his new found answers among a doubtful circle of family and acquaintances. His confidence might be misplaced, but he isn’t cynical. When he tells Scott, a depressed young man played by Stephen McMillan who comes to see him, all he’s learnt and how he wants to help he’s genuine. “He really means that when he’s saying that Marshall saved him from a very dark place,” says Nicoll. “That is, I think, a crucial part of the character.” Over the course of the film, “the economic imperative kind of takes over,” altering the relationship between Danny and Scott as the former discovers the wordplay he absorbed as self-help can turn into a tool for manipulation. The result is a chain of unequal relationships: Marshall has power over Danny, while Danny gains power over Scott. For Nicoll, that dynamic goes beyond any single strain of digital culture. “Most people could probably relate to the idea of when you go online and someone’s telling you how to eat better or exercise better or be happier, be in a better relationship,” he said. At a moment of insecurity, the promise that somebody else knows how to sort it can prove hard to resist. Nicoll had previously directed Liam Harkins in short “Lighting Tests” and wrote Danny around a rare combination he saw in the actor: an outwardly conventional masculinity alongside vulnerability, sensitivity and comedic timing. “I had the idea for the story and thought he would be perfect for the role,” said Nicoll, who sent drafts back and forth to Harkins roughly a year before shooting. “I knew that on a production standpoint, he would just be the rock that could build the production around.” The relationship at the film’s centre needed warmth as well as exploitation. The director recalls nervously arranging a Zoom between his two leads prior to filming, preparing questions in case conversation petered out. “I think I probably said about three things in the hour,” he says. “They were just chatting, getting to know each other, and then just talking about the characters.” A later read-through of three key scenes confirmed the chemistry: “It was an amazing one of being like, ‘Oh, we’ve got something here.’” That closeness is gradually squeezed by the film’s visual language. Working with cinematographer Alex Grigoras, Nicoll chose a 4:3 frame. “We always knew it was going to be a film of faces,” he says. The format offered intimacy and, as Danny’s choices reduce, claustrophobia. Centering him clarifies his self-absorption. He is initially, “the centre of his own world.” The use of long lenses compress the spaces around him, particularly in the interiors, while stillness releases giving way to unsettled camerawork as the predicament deteriorates. Composer Salla Luhtala’s score pushes in almost the opposite direction. At the start, as Danny leaves the retreat filled with new conviction, the music enlarges his modest circumstances matching the way he sees himself. “It’s like the world is his oyster. That’s what he feels like,” Nicoll explained. “It should feel like he’s reborn. It should feel like new momentum. It should feel like the new life is calling him.” Rather than standing outside Danny and mocking the fantasy, Nicoll wanted audiences pulled into it. “Salvation” is as Indie as it gets assembled through self-financing and crowdfunding, with Screen Scotland boarding late and providing £45,000 ($60,750) through its Production Growth Fund. Shot around Greenock and Glasgow, the production initially completed 15 days before returning months later for a few more days. “That’s the nature of independent filmmaking, I suppose,” he says. But the enforced pause became “an amazing opportunity,” allowing a chance to clarify the story and add “scale and cinematic scope at the right moments.” Nicoll looked to an American independent tradition for ways of making those limitations feel like choices. Sean Baker’s “Red Rocket” and earlier work were reference points, as was Kelly Reichardt’s “Old Joy”: films capable of retaining a distinct voice without requiring vast resources. And what of that word “Salvation”? “It’s the kind of underpinning, I think, of a lot of these self-help ideas,” says Nicoll. “You can be saved from this thing, and you can move into a kind of hallowed place, or a place free of this previous pain or this previous deficiency. And I don’t know if I believe in that.” The film isn’t interested in providing a clean, moralistic conclusion. The director prefers films that resist “easy answers,” leaving open the question of whether Danny is capable of deep reflection or likely to place explanations for everything that has happened to him elsewhere. For a film that Nicoll describes as “an independent film in its bones,” there is buzz around it. MetFilm Sales’ acquisition adds a strong international sales push to a run that has included Great 8 and selection as one of Screen International’s Rising Stars Scotland 2026. “It’s been pretty wild,” Nicoll said. “It’s pretty much close to best-case scenario” for a film made this way. More importantly, he adds, “it is the film I wanted to make.” The recognition offers the possibility of scaling up, something the writer-director is keen to pursue as he looks to move beyond the indie and micro-budget level. He has several scripts in various stages, including larger-scale thriller and horror projects. “Ambition can be talked about just as it relates to budget, but I think it’s about your approach to characters and characterisation, and how deep you’re willing to go in terms of excavating what it is to be human,” he says. “That’s what ambition is about in filmmaking to me, and that’s what I would want to take going forward, no matter the level of budget.” Outsider Pictures Takes U.S. on Rafiki Fariala’s Award-Winning Cannes Hit ‘Congo Boy’ (EXCLUSIVE) Cannes’ Critics’ Week Reveals Lineup of Armenian Filmmakers Taking Part in Next Step Studio Program (EXCLUSIVE) Bruno Dumont’s Cannes Movie ‘Red Rocks’ Sells to North America (EXCLUSIVE) Wim-Wenders Produced ‘I’ll Be Gone in June’ Bought for North America After Cannes Premiere (EXCLUSIVE) Sundance Prizewinner Blerta Basholli on Kosovar War Drama ‘Dua’: ‘Teenagers Growing Up in Conflict Zones Are No Different From Any of Us’ France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets Loading comments... title: Yoon Dan-bi’s Toronto and San Sebastian Film ‘The World Before’ Gives Its Camera a Soul and Its Island a Voice
full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:21am PT Yoon Dan-bi’s Toronto and San Sebastian Film ‘The World Before’ Gives Its Camera a Soul and Its Island a Voice By Ophélie Surcouf Plus Icon Ophélie Surcouf Latest Stephanie Ahn’s Seven-Year Road to ‘Bedford Park’: ‘You Never Know What Can Make Your Film Better’ 2 days ago Hyun Bin and Woo Do-hwan Turn Against Each Other in Hulu and Disney+’s ‘Made in Korea’ Season 2 2 weeks ago Cortis and Airbnb Color Outside the Lines With Immersive Seoul Hideout 5 months ago See All 'The World Before' Courtesy of the Toronto Film Festival Seven years after “Moving On,” Korean filmmaker Yoon Dan-bi returns with “ The World Before ,” a coming-of-age film about desire and first love. Speaking with Variety ahead of the film’s Toronto Film Festival Platform world premiere, Yoon discusses how capturing the authenticity of change worked its way at every stage of the production. “I want to make films about things that can’t be described in one sentence,” says Yoon. “In my previous movie I wanted to capture nostalgia, here I wanted to capture the restlessness, that fever you experience when innocence turns into desire.” Related Stories ‘Back to Buenos Aires’ Review: Marco Bechis’ Return to the Screen Covers Similar Ground to Earlier Works but is Only Fitfully Effective Netflix’s YA Rowing Drama 'Crew Girl' Capsizes and Sinks: TV Review The coming-of-age story follows 17-year-old Jin and her unexpected reunion with childhood friend Du-jae, who returns for his grandmother’s funeral on a remote Korean island. For Yoon, narrating the chapter that marks the end of childhood and the beginning of adulthood required focusing on her character’s inner turmoil, but also very much on their physicality. Popular on Variety “As well as emotion, I’m very keen on observing people’s movement,” she explains. “When the feeling of desire is born, how does it affect movement? How do they let their guard down when they love, hug each other, unexpectedly hold hands? I wanted to portray that desire in a very realistic way, without being overtly sexual.” That attention changed drastically how she used the camera. While ‘Moving On’’s stationary and observational lens blurred the line so well between reality and fiction that many commented it felt it was a documentary, Yoon tried another technique in “The World Before.” “The camera moves around a lot as if it had its own soul,” says Yoon. “I wanted to move it unexpectedly to create a rhythm. For example, there’s a scene on the beach with Jin and Du-jae where you see the light coming in, then the sun goes behind the clouds and comes out again. It was all natural light when we were shooting,” she pauses to laugh. “My crew told me this effect can be done in post production, but I tend not to believe them and I prefer to wait.” Yoon is grateful to her crew, who she says had a hard time rescheduling shoots, staged across two islands during the hot, humid months of the Korean summer, when a typhoon came around. They also had to carry all the equipment without cars as Soan-do, one of the islands located in Wando County off the southern coast, had no bridge connecting to the mainland. “We wanted rain scenes,” she adds, “but it didn’t rain that summer.” Still, Yoon loves the aesthetics of this period which she describes as the season of growing up. Lulled by the chant of cicadas, the island’s bright stillness offers the perfect contrast to the movement Yoon chases – light inching on naked skin and leaves blowing in the wind. “Soando feels very much like how the countryside used to be in Korea,” Yoon notes. “The main labor there is fishing abalone and seaweed, they’re pretty much self sufficient. The villagers offered help and invited us for food, which helped the actors to adapt to island life quickly. But looking back, I realized I went with a sort of prejudice, I thought everyone would want to escape but it turns out they all wanted to stay there.” The correction found its way into the character: “Jin likes living on the island and doesn’t even consider leaving,” Yoon says. Other surprises made it into the film as well – a local grandmother was cast for the opening scene after the villagers pronounced her the best singer among them ; an improvised moment between the young leads watching ants by the roadside, became one of the movie’s authentic snippets of life. But those additions are only possible because the script is written to accommodate them. “I tend to revise my script a lot while shooting, and I write it with that process in mind,” Yoon says. “That’s why I prefer to film in chronological order so I can really connect to the following scene. Of course, it doesn’t always work as I intend to,” she laughs. Another ingredient of her movie’s authenticity is her casting process. She found the central pair, Sim Su-bin (“Teach You a Lesson,” “Filing for Love”) in the role of Jin, and first timer Kim Eo-jin as Du-jae through auditions. Both are relatively unfamiliar faces, even to Korean audiences, so Yoon built the surrounding ensemble to help them carry the film. “I was worried that if the older actors were too famous, they’d take the focus away from them, so I needed to balance this,” she says. Once shooting began, she made a point to let her young leads embody the material. “As in my previous film, an emerging actor was playing the protagonist, so if the actor prefers to do a scene in a different way than I envisioned, I try to adapt,” Yoon explains. “I encourage the actors to find the intimacy that feels right for them. I know how they talk and behave, I don’t want them to stick to the script but use their own words.” Only the second Korean film selected for the section after Yoon Ga-eun’s “The World of Love” last year, “The World Before” will be headed to the San Sebastian Film Festival ‘s New Directors competition later this month. title: ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation
full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:20am PT ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation Filmmaker Bertil Nilsson creates a grammar for masculinity in collaboration with his lead actor Joshua Griffin. By Murtada Elfadl Plus Icon Murtada Elfadl Latest ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation 2 hours ago ‘What Will I Become?’ Review: Transmasculine Lives Take Center Stage in a Poignant Portrait of Loss 4 weeks ago ‘Bouchra’ Review: Animated Memoir Explores Diasporic Queer Identity and the Fraught Bonds Between Mothers and Daughters 3 months ago See All Duktiga Ltd In “ Masc ,” director Bertil Nilsson pulls off a nifty trick: He observes an observer. Usually a film’s protagonist has the dominant POV, but here, Robin (Joshua Griffin) is trying to find his personality by observing other men in his orbit. He almost never initiates the action and is mostly reticent about his reactions, but he takes note of everything. This makes for a fascinating watching experience for the audience, as they find themselves in Robin’s shoes, trying to figure out how to behave. In the process “Masc” becomes a thoroughly unique experience. Related Stories 'Boatbuilders' Review: A Mellow Maine Boatyard Study That Offers All the Quiet Rewards of Fine Craftsmanship in Action ‘The Fire Within You’ Review: An Insufferable Christmas Eve Family Drama in Which the Corrosive Rants Are as Noxious as the Dyspeptic Images Robin is queer, biracial and neurodivergent, so society forces multiple identities on him. In the span of a year, he changes his appearance five times and tries on different jobs, places and people to hang out with. He works as an apprentice handyman and lab assistant, tries to immerse himself within a therapy group and seeks camaraderie with different guys his age. In the process, he takes on their mannerisms and models his personality on them, tries to figure out why they behave the way they do. It’s an intense journey that’s also internal; the strength of the film, and of Griffin’s performance, lies in how tangible and visceral they make that progress. Popular on Variety Nilsson wrote “Masc” based on a story he crafted with Griffin, and it plays as an organic collaboration between filmmaker and actor. Whether or not they improvised the situations that they put Robin in together, those play so naturally that the film sometimes has the feel of an observational documentary, which is exactly as it should be with such a sensitive character study. But “Masc” is also clearly a work of fiction. Not only does Nilsson place the audience in Robin’s purview, he also creates scenes that tell us how he imagines things, how he wishes situations would transpire. In one immaculately crafted and tenderly portrayed scene, Robin stays overnight with a friend, Benji (Tega Alexander). The audience is privy to his vacillating feelings about his friend, how he hopes the night will go, and what he fears it might become. It is a vivid portrait of his innermost feelings and anxieties. Griffin is tremendous, carrying the film on his shoulders as he appears in almost every frame. He has amazing physical control, making even the solitary scenes captivating; his presence, both jittery and grounded, conveys the complexity of Robin’s constant observation and recording of other people. When he is alone, there’s clear relief in the easier, more rhythmic way he moves. In closeup, his eyes broadcast all that the character is feeling; always watchful, always taking note of everything and everyone. The performance makes a moving and empathetic endeavor of the character’s search for a blueprint of life and personality. Griffin’s vulnerability is most pronounced in a long scene where Robin spends time with his father (Lincoln Conway) — finally, he is not observing and just being, even if he’s not entirely comfortable. He still has fears of being unloved, but he’s at his most unguarded. Perhaps this familiar form of masculinity is the one he’s been searching for all along. What makes “Masc” compelling is the way Nilsson turns observation into a mode of self-construction. Robin studies the men around him as though they might offer a grammar for being, borrowing their gestures, routines and affect in an attempt to locate something stable within himself. Yet the film understands identity not as something waiting to be discovered, but as something continually negotiated through imitation, desire and rejection. “Masc” shows that for those who exist outside prescribed ideas of masculinity, becoming oneself can first require learning how to read everyone else. ‘Masc’ Review: A Sensitive Character Study Where Identity is Found in Imitation and Observation Reviewed online, Sept. 9, 2026. title: Shuhua’s Acting Debut and Breaking Free From the ‘American Girl’ Label: Director Feng-i Fiona Roan on Toronto Title ‘Happily Ever After’
full_text: Sep 13, 2026 4:11am PT Shuhua’s Acting Debut and Breaking Free From the ‘American Girl’ Label: Director Feng-i Fiona Roan on Toronto Title ‘Happily Ever After’ By Lin Ying-Hsuan Plus Icon Lin Ying-Hsuan Latest Taiwan Strengthens Global Co-Production Presence at Toronto Film Festival With ‘Happily Ever After,’ ‘The Age of Goodbyes’ and ‘Arrested Memory‘ 24 hours ago Sam Worthington, David Duchovny and Ke-Xi Wu’s ‘The Exiles’ Inspired by Joseph Conrad’s ‘Heart of Darkness,’ Director Midi Z Reveals (EXCLUSIVE) 2 months ago Wu Jing Honored at MIFFest, Says Hong Kong Action Cinema’s Influence Still Runs Through Every Wuxia Film Today 2 months ago See All Happily Ever After Toronto Film Festival “ Happily Ever After ,” the follow-up feature from Taiwanese director Feng-i Fiona Roan , is bowing in the Toronto Film Festival ’s Special Presentations lineup, arriving amid heightened attention following the success of her acclaimed debut, “American Girl.” “American Girl” premiered in the Asian Future section of the Tokyo International Film Festival before earning seven Golden Horse Award nominations and winning three prizes, including best new director. During the Golden Horse celebrations, Roan received a gentle but prescient warning from Oscar-winning filmmaker Ang Lee. Related Stories ‘Stuffed’ Review: Jodie Comer and Harry Melling Sing the Body Eccentric in an Odd, and Oddly Touching, Taxidermy Musical 'NAZA' Review: Two of the 'No Other Land' Filmmakers Deliver a More Devastating Exposé of Israeli Genocidal Policy, This Time in Gaza “Director Ang Lee reminded me that the second film is always the hardest,” Roan tells Variety . “Being able to present my second feature at TIFF as its first stop is very meaningful to me. I also hope it can open up more conversations and opportunities.” Popular on Variety Drawn from Roan’s childhood and family history, “American Girl” earned widespread acclaim but also prompted some observers to question whether the filmmaker could move beyond autobiography. “From the development stage of ‘Happily Ever After,’ I was determined to break away from that label,” Roan says. “I was entering a different phase of my life and was even planning my own wedding at the time. This fictional story went from nothing to a complete screenplay within a year, but it also captured the emotional shifts that my friends and I were experiencing at different stages of our lives.” “Happily Ever After” closely examines the subtle emotional dynamics between two sisters. The story initially placed greater emphasis on the younger sister, played by Shuhua, before evolving into a dual-protagonist narrative. “While developing the screenplay, I watched ‘Frozen’ for a second time and suddenly realized how remarkably well it balances the narrative arcs of its two sister protagonists,” Roan says. “I went back and analyzed the screenplay for that reason, then used what I learned to refine the rhythm of my own script.” Beyond the expectations surrounding Roan’s second feature, the film has attracted attention across the film, television and music industries for casting K-pop star Shuhua in her film debut. “When we met Shuhua, we only asked her to read two scenes,” Roan says. “Her confidence and personality came through so naturally that we decided on the spot.” During production, Roan sought to create an authentic sense of family among the cast. Rather than addressing Shuhua by her real name or her character’s name, everyone on set simply called her “little sister.” Before filming began, Shuhua was also invited to name the cat that appears as the family pet. Shuhua’s own experience as the middle child in a family of three daughters gave her a deeper emotional connection to the role, according to Roan. “I gave her only one note: Before making any movement or delivering any line, she had to have a motivation,” Roan says. “Only after you have convinced yourself can your performance move the audience.” Asked how she hopes international audiences will view contemporary Taiwanese cinema, Roan draws on her experience living in the U.S. and her observations from attending international film festivals. “Filmmakers from the previous generation, such as Hou Hsiao-hsien and Edward Yang, naturally still have enormous international visibility,” she says. “Their particular time and circumstances allowed them to pursue their artistic practices to an extremely high degree, and those achievements have secured their place in film history.” Roan believes her own generation brings a stronger awareness of genre and a greater willingness to experiment with different forms. “Every festival feels a little like a social experiment,” she says. “We bring different stories to international audiences and observe how they respond and what kinds of thoughts those stories provoke.” Alongside the classics of Taiwanese cinema, Roan cites French New Wave pioneer Agnès Varda as a formative influence. She also points to Ozu Yasujirō’s cycle of films about fathers marrying off their daughters, Kore-eda Hirokazu’s family dramas and Greta Gerwig’s explorations of women’s inner lives. “My favorite film this year is ‘The World of Love,’ by South Korean director Yoon Ga-eun,” Roan says. During the early development of “Happily Ever After,” Roan immersed herself in reading, including Taiwanese author Kevin Chen’s novel “Ghost Town.” Stories exploring family, identity and self-worth fed into her new fictional direction while allowing her to retain the emotional honesty of her earlier work. As the film meets its first international audience in Toronto, Roan is eager to exchange ideas with filmmakers from around the world. Above all, she hopes “Happily Ever After” will spark a conversation around the question embedded in its title: What does it mean to be happy on your own terms?
