title: ‘Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom’ Review: The Third Time’s Charming, Just Like the First and Second
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Frank Scheck Plus Icon Frank Scheck View All September 13, 2026 4:00am 'Shaun The Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom' It’s a little early for Halloween, but that hasn’t stopped the creators of Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom from delivering their creepiest feature yet. Not to worry that it will scare youngsters, however, since this third film in the hit franchise spun off from Aardman Animation’s Wallace & Gromit series is just as delightful as its predecessors. Delivering the same sort of droll, deadpan British humor via stop-motion animation as 2015’s Shaun the Sheep Movie and 2019’s A Shaun the Sheep Movie: Farmageddon , this installment could easily become the third to receive an Oscar nomination for best animated film. Related Stories TV Pokémon Stop-Motion Series Set at Disney+ as Part of Larger Distribution Deal Movies A Hairy Monster Threatens The Flock in Trailer for New 'Shaun the Sheep' Movie The story is set a few days before the holiday, when the farmer and his flock are eagerly preparing for the Halloween Hoedown, with Shaun the Sheep (Justin Fletcher) proudly hanging up his offspring Timmy’s drawing of a pumpkin. The farmer (John Sparkes) has a big crush on the local veterinarian (Nina Sosanya, voicing a new and welcome human character), who keeps finding strange objects in her patients’ bodies. But he’s afraid to ask her to the hoedown because he’s embarrassed about his encroaching hair loss. Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom The Bottom Line As usual, a drolly amusing delight. Release date : Friday, Sept. 18 Cast : Justin Fletcher, John Sparkes, Kate Harbour, Dani Dyer, Roman Kemp, Nina Sosanya, Paul Whitehouse Directors : Steve Cox, Matthew Walker Screenwriters : Mark Burton, Giles Pilbrow 1 hour 20 minutes When the farmer accidentally destroys his flock’s beloved pumpkin patch, Shaun attempts to remedy things by conducting a few experiments after he reads an introductory science book. While he succeeds in restoring the pumpkins, the well-meaning sheep’s efforts go awry, causing the farmer’s hair-growth lotion to have the unintended effect of making him sprout hair in inappropriate places and eventually covering his entire body with thick, matted orange fur. Needless to say, the farmer’s attempts to rectify the situation with his electric razor are for naught. As the Beast of Mossy Bottom roams the countryside spurring fear and panic, the intrepid veterinarian attempts to solve the mystery, convinced that the creature she’s tracking is Bigfoot. The farmer’s loyal canine sidekick Bitzer (Sparkes), desperate to find his missing master, gets involved as well. Meanwhile, the farmer’s attempt to remove his excess hair with duct tape proves painful enough to produce monstrous howls. It’s all sheer silliness, of course, and that’s the point, with the dialogue-free storyline providing the possibilities not only for endless cuteness — these painstakingly moved puppets, representing both human and animal characters, are truly adorable — but also a series of witty visual and sound gags that will please children and adults alike. The former will delight in the big-eyed animal shenanigans, while the latter will enjoy a great gag about the unintelligibility of parking signs and the amusing sight of a particularly large sheep proudly erasing a blackboard with her wool. One of the film’s funniest scenes features the Beast taking refuge in a Halloween shop and trying to blend in with life-size figures of the Mummy and Dracula. Much as its predecessor riffed on sci-fi movie themes and clichés, this installment finds fodder in horror films with jokes inspired by everything from Frankenstein to the “Thriller” video to Psycho (there’s a shower scene, with the sounds of a sheep flossing replacing Bernard Herrmann’s piercing strings). While not everything works, the gags come at such a fast pace that you’re never bored. And unlike the frenetic, in-your-face style of so many American animated films, the charmingly low-key Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom always feels understated, as if slightly embarrassed when the humor becomes lowbrow. The fun isn’t just in the images. The performers’ non-verbal voice work, the inventive sound effects and the amusing musical selections add greatly to the fun as well. title: Inside ‘NAZA,’ the Bombshell Exposé on IDF’s War in Gaza
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close 'NAZA' Naza/The Guardian NAZA , which won a Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival Saturday night , is already one of the most shocking and controversial documentaries of the year. It may also prove to be one of the most indispensable. The exposé, from Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, features testimony from 24 Israeli military officers outlining the systems and protocols they allege Israel uses to target and kill civilians in Gaza. The film’s title, NAZA , comes from an acronym the Israeli military uses as a shorthand for civilian casualties. Related Stories TIFF RISING STAR 'Happily Ever After' Star Shuhua Yeh Makes the Leap From K-pop Idol to Actress: "It's Really Happening" Toronto Rising Stars 'Look Back' Breakouts Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada on Growing Up on a Hirokazu Koreeda Set Abraham and Szor, part of the director collective behind the Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land , which documented the destruction of a village in the occupied West Bank by Israeli soldiers and settlers, shot NAZA clandestinely over three years, doing the interviews under the cover of night on the rooftops of Tel Aviv. The duo used VFX to alter the voices and faces of the officers. Their allegations and revelations are harrowing. One describes hacking into the phone of a 12-year-old girl to identify when her father, a target, comes home, and ordering the bombing that kills the whole family. Another describes how snipers gun down Palestinian civilians as they desperately scramble to reach a food distribution site. NAZA was enthusiastically received in Venice with a 25-minute standing ovation, an all-time record. Jonathan Glazer, the Oscar-winning director of The Zone of Interest , executive produced the film. Mk2 Films is handling worldwide sales. In a statement, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “categorically rejects” the film’s allegations and criticized the use of anonymous testimonies, which it said “cannot be verified.” It repeated claims that “the IDF strikes military targets and makes unprecedented efforts to minimize harm to civilians.” Abraham and Szor spoke to The Hollywood Reporter on the making of the film, fighting the “complicity of silence” and whether their film can bring about real-world change. “Because this is not something of the past. It’s still ongoing.” The film builds on investigative work you did with The Guardian , the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine , and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call between 2023 and 2025. How did that collaboration come about? Yuval Abraham: The film is built on investigative work that I’ve done together with colleagues at The Guardian , like Harry Davies and Emma Graham-Harrison and others, who — we’ve been looking at the way the Israeli targeting systems work, Israeli mass surveillance over Palestinians, and how mass killing works. And me and Rachel, of course, we worked on No Other Land together with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, and we realized that we wanted to make a film that is in this intersection between cinema and journalism. I think a film allows us to examine the system, the systemic nature of the killing in Gaza — and we knew that we wanted to have a very rigorous process of journalism, of fact-checking, of scrutinizing the work that we were doing, and The Guardian and The Guardian ‘s investigations desk were very valuable in that sense, to partner with us on this. How did you find these 24 officers who speak to you so openly in the documentary, and how did you convince them to speak? Abraham: It was a process. It took months, and in some instances years, to find people and to speak with them. For some of them, it took a long time until they decided to agree to speak in front of a camera. I think people were aware that what they are exposing is quite damning information on the Israeli state crimes that were perpetrated in Gaza. And if you think about the fact that Israel, to this day, is not letting international journalists enter Gaza to witness what human rights organizations across the world are calling a genocide — much of the burden is placed on Palestinian journalists, who have been killed. You know, 200 of them have been killed. So I think it’s obviously for this reason that people were afraid, because it’s clear that the Israeli government is trying to block these attempts at accountability, whether it’s through assassinating and killing Palestinian journalists or through other means, by preventing international journalists from coming in. So it was a challenge, but ultimately, when you’re an investigative journalist, you build a network of sources. You move from one person to the next. You have to be patient sometimes and let people make up their own minds. It was important for us that the people participating give their informed consent, and we knew that we would have to rely on a large group of sources — because this film is making quite heavy claims about how Israel’s system of targeting works, about the fact that attacking civilian spaces, family homes, is something that is built into the system by design. It’s looking for targets when they come back to their homes. ‘NAZA’ directors Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham Barol/Anadolu via Getty Images The fact that there were protocols that soldiers operated by, of shooting and killing anybody they saw on the ground in large areas, including women and children — I don’t know if this was a written protocol, but many, many soldiers said that this was the logic they were operating by. So to credibly make those claims in a documentary, we knew we would need many sources. So this is why we also had to get two dozen of them for this film. The other thing that I would want to add is that I think these policies, and the truth of these policies, should have been evident without relying on Israeli soldiers. Palestinians have been documenting this on the ground from the very first day. You don’t have to be a genius to realize that when children come into hospitals with sniper wounds, and Palestinians are documenting it, that they’re being intentionally shot by soldiers. Between May and late October 2025, Palestinians were documenting massacre after massacre happening at the food sites, the GHF sites — you didn’t have to wait for the soldiers who appear in our film, describing how they would see snipers shooting at unarmed civilians running toward food in front of the camera, to know that this is true. That truth should have been evident from the very start, and I think, because so many people — especially Israelis, and people in the United States and in Germany and other places — are still denying those crimes, and because the denial of those crimes allows them to persist, we felt it was important to also bring insider testimony from the people who design those systems, from the people who operated those systems. Because it’s ongoing. It’s not something of the past. It’s something that’s very much rooted in the present, and we hope will not continue more and more into the future. What did the people who agreed to speak with you say were their reasons for doing so? Rachel Szor: In the film there are 24 different people speaking, so there’s a range of reasons why people want to speak. We also talked about it between ourselves: what is their motive to come to us? The film touches on it a bit. There are some people that perhaps feel some sort of responsibility, and they also wanted to speak about it in Hebrew so that more Israelis will hear about it. Some people in the film, you see, feel some sort of pride [in what they did]. We don’t really know what the psychological reasons are. I feel that perhaps it’s also because not many people are asking these questions. In Israel, in the mainstream media, no one really talks about it. There are a few journalists who investigate those things, but no one really gives those soldiers the stage. It’s really like a secret topic, especially the intelligence around it, no one really talks about it. So it was kind of the first time they could speak about it was when they spoke about it with Yuval. The film is less about trying to solve the question of why they spoke out, or how Yuval got to them; it’s really more about them describing the systems they use for the mass killing. (L to R): Jonathan Glazer, Rachel Szor, Yuval Abraham and producer James Wilson attend the “NAZA” photocall at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival Aurore Marechal/Getty Images How did Jonathan Glazer get involved in this project as an executive producer? Abraham: We met Jonathan for the first time with No Other Land . He hosted a Q&A, and we connected afterward. We were really influenced by The Zone of Interest . I remember hearing Jonathan say that in that film, the victims were out of sight, but they were never out of mind for a second. That really, I think, informed how we were thinking of the cinematic language and the way we structured NAZA — the fact that we are looking at an Israeli city, Tel Aviv, we are looking at Israelis involved in mass killings, and the victims, for most of the film, are out of sight. But they’re never out of mind, in the sense that the reason for being of this film is the crimes committed against the Palestinians in Gaza. This was our motivation, and this is also what we were interested in exploring — how those systems look, and what allows people to participate in them. You’ve both been investigating these types of crimes for some time, in different forms, including with your last film. Was there anything surprising or shocking for you that came out of these interviews and this investigation? Abraham: I’m not sure if it was surprising, again, because the truth of what is happening in Gaza could have been evident, and should have been evident, from the start. If you listen to the openly genocidal statements of Israeli ministers, senior figures in the government, senior military officials — I mean, just recently, our defense minister, Israel Katz, said that the only solution for Gaza is migration, and the government is ready to do it by air, by land, or by sea, in any way possible. This kind of rhetoric makes clear that the intent is the removal of Palestinians, and the dehumanization has been on the table. It could have been clear from the start, if people listened to Palestinians, to civilians in Gaza, to journalists who have been documenting it. So I can’t say there was a surprise at the revelations in the film. I think what was striking was hearing how much these tools are already built on a logic that is extremely deadly for civilians. We look at one kind of protocol of operation, a tool called Where’s Daddy, which is a system that, by spying on family members of people the Israeli military wants to kill, waits until a family member says the person is home, and the system is built on bombing those individuals when they are in their family homes, when they are sleeping, at night. What was really striking about this to me is that you so often hear the way the international media and the Israeli media frame this killing as ‘okay, we are bombing them because Hamas is using them as human shields.’ You imagine that Hamas is firing rockets out of those civilian houses, and this is why they are bombed. And we have soldiers in our film saying Hamas uses human shields in some cases, but the majority of the killing — this mass slaughter of civilians inside their homes — is not because the homes are used as human shields. It’s because this is how the Israeli targeting system is built. It’s because the goal — a genocidal goal, in my mind, from the start — was to destroy these so-called targets, with AI involved in selecting those targets, and that civilian spaces are routinely bombed by design. These are practices and methods that existed already before the massacre of October 7, but afterward they were applied and pushed to such an extreme that the inevitable, pre-calculated, premeditated results are, as we know, that more than 2,900 families in Gaza, multiple generations, were just completely erased, all the members of the family murdered. This was part of the logic of how the Israeli system operated. What was it like, personally, to conduct these interviews with people admitting to war crimes? Abraham: Yeah, it’s a challenge, because I know that as an interviewer, you don’t really need to push the person talking in order to get to the truth. All you have to ask, really, once the person is sitting in front of you, is: describe to me what you did, how did systems work? Because the truth of what happened in Gaza is so horrible, just asking is sometimes enough. I actually think you need to use quite a lot of manipulation if you want to obscure that truth, if you want to reframe it in a way where it is not clear — that is the difficult task. The film is based on more than 100 hours of interview material, and every story or claim that is made in the film is something that we heard again and again, from multiple people and multiple sources. I felt it was important to interview them in that way so that the audience feels this film is as factual, as objective as possible, because it is also some kind of document. Of course, we have our personal opinions. We’ve made them clear. But I know that the people I want to reach, the people who need to change, the people whose silence or complicity is allowing the crimes to persist, are maybe people who don’t agree with my conclusions. There are Israeli elections coming up — do you expect this film and its revelations to affect the debate, or even the result of the elections? Szor: Yeah, we really don’t know. Of course, we hope that it will be shown in Israel and will have as much influence as possible. But unfortunately, in this election, what’s happening in Gaza — still ongoing every week — and what’s happening in the West Bank is just not a topic, an issue, in the elections. So it’s a big question for us as well, how the film will be received in Israel. But we hope that the fact that it’s soldiers from the system speaking in Hebrew will perhaps have some sort of influence. ‘No Other Land’ Courtesy of Sheffield DocFest Will it be released in Israel? Do you have a distributor there? Abraham: We don’t have a distributor yet, but it’s definitely our intention to release it as widely as possible in Israel, and in the United States, and in Germany. As I said, I think it’s our responsibility — we are Israelis, we come from that society, and we are citizens of the country that is committing these grave crimes, and we want to confront that, and show and share this with people from the place we come from, and also around the world. We will try. We can’t know if there will be mainstream platforms in Israel, but we want to take this film there. I think it’s definitely important for us, because I feel it’s our responsibility to do this work. Your last film No Other Land had difficulty getting distributed in the U.S. and other territories. Do you expect similar resistance from mainstream distributors with this film? Abraham: I don’t know — it’s kind of too early to tell. My gut tells me, and I hope I’m wrong on this, that it will be just as difficult. I know there are important public opinion changes in the United States. I think there will be a big audience for this film, especially in the United States, since the killing was carried out with weapons that were created in the U.S., funded by U.S. taxpayer money — $21.7 billion worth of arms and equipment sent to Israel since October 7, which is still being carried out. Just this week, a seven-year-old girl in Gaza was killed with her father in her car. This is all being done thanks to the support of the United States, and the refusal of consecutive U.S. governments to condition or suspend completely the arms they send to Israel. So it’s so important for us that people in the United States really listen to the Israeli officers and soldiers describing how their weapons were used. And I hope there will be a mainstream distributor that takes this film and carries it into the United States. I don’t know that it’s going to happen, but I hope it will. More generally, what level of risk is there — for you, and for the people who participated in this film — of being prosecuted or targeted by the Israeli government because of these revelations? Abraham: There is someone in the film who says they want to hide their identity because they are afraid of retaliation and imprisonment by the Israeli government. Israel’s government is a far-right government, and we know that they are not letting international journalists into Gaza, and they’ve killed so many Palestinian journalists there. So it’s clear there is an intent to obscure or hide the truth, and there’s something about that truth appearing through the voices of people inside that system that I’m guessing the state will be very unhappy about, and will try to block from coming out. But at the same time, I can speak for myself and Rachel — I think there is nothing wrong in what we are doing. I think it’s what we should be doing as journalists, and what we should be doing as humans, and as citizens of a country that is committing such crimes. So I hope that we will not have to pay a certain kind of price for it. (L to R): The directors of ‘No Other Land’: Basel Adra, Rachel Szor, Hamdan Ballal, and Yuval Abraham Mike Coppola/Getty Images Given the backlash you faced after your last film, and given that Gaza and the occupied territories aren’t playing a major role in this election, does that discourage you? Rachel Szor: I think the question is less about the backlash and more about the impact. With No Other Land , we won the Oscar, as a collective, and it’s the biggest award you can get, and we felt so many people watched it — but still, this week, two villages were destroyed in a-Safai al-Tahta, and that’s exactly what the film was about — this policy of removing and destroying the houses of Palestinians in that area — and it’s still happening. So, in a way, you ask yourself what kind of impact it can have. But so many people, greater than us, are doing things, and you’re never sure what impact it will have. We have this privilege as Israelis to bring these testimonies in the film. It was less a question of whether we despair or not and more the feeling that we have to do it. Yuval Abraham: I think Rachel and I think realize we are operating in a system of Jewish-Israeli supremacy and privilege. When our Palestinian journalist colleagues in Gaza are really paying with their lives — so many have been killed and murdered by Israel for documenting what is happening around them — to me, it’s clear that there is an importance to documentation. In our film, No Other Land , Basel is still continuing to document what was happening to his community. He says that change can sometimes be like water dropping — drop after drop after drop — and eventually there will be a change. We hope so. For me, I think a lot of this change has to start with a change in U.S. foreign policy, and I hope that the film can contribute to that somehow. This interview was edited for length and clarity. THR

title: ‘Happily Ever After’ Star Shuhua Yeh Makes the Leap From K-pop Idol to Actress: “It’s Really Happening”
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close Shuhua stars as Kitty in 'Happily Ever After.' Courtesy of Cube Entertainment Happily Ever After star Shuhua Yeh might be a fresh face in the acting world, but she’s no stranger to the global stage. Making her acting debut in Feng-I Fiona Roan’s sophomore outing, which is having its world premiere in Toronto, she’s finally achieving a goal that’s been in the cards for her since her high school days. “I was aiming to become an actress at first,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter on a late night — actually, early morning — Zoom call from her home in Seoul. Yeh, who grew up in Taoyuan, Taiwan, and attended an arts high school in Taipei, where she majored in drama. She spent much of her young life believing her career in entertainment — which was always a certainty — would begin with acting and then she’d branch out. Things didn’t quite go to plan. Related Stories Toronto Rising Stars 'Look Back' Breakouts Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada on Growing Up on a Hirokazu Koreeda Set Movies Toronto Awards Analysis: 'I Play Rocky' Channels Namesake, Could Follow in Its Oscar Footsteps Yeh ended up moving to Korea and began training to become a K-pop idol under Cube Entertainment. She debuted in the girl group I-dle, formerly known as (G)I-dle, in 2018. The group found quick domestic success and has continued to rack up hit after hit in Korea and beyond. Despite her brief interlude from acting while amassing international success as a pop star, Yeh hasn’t found the transition to be that difficult. K-pop tends to lean into plot-based album concepts, so she had the opportunity to develop her craft while working on music videos. “It somehow feels like picking up something from my childhood,” Yeh says. “It feels exciting rather than very challenging. I can finally demonstrate the things I have in my toolbox.” In Happily Ever After , Yeh plays Kitty, one of the two sisters at the center of this family-focused film. Kitty’s the younger sister and the ideal daughter — depending on your definition — alongside Xuan Chen’s Claire. When a stray cat wanders into their lives, long-dormant tensions bubble up to the surface. The film explores the burden of expectations that families can place on young people. Yeh as Kitty in ‘Happily Ever After.’ Splash Pictures, Inc When Yeh first read the script, she wasn’t sure which of the two roles was intended for her but felt that Kitty’s personality was quite the opposite of her own — a prospect she found exciting. She wanted, she says, a bit of challenge and more room to play with. Yeh initially met up with Roan and a producer to discuss the film, where the director shared the story of her family and her sisters. Sisterhood sits at the center of the film and Yeh, herself the middle child of three sisters, found it easy to relate the material to her own life. Throughout the process of making Happily Ever After, Yeh not only drew from her own family experiences — she also came to see her own family in a new light. “I sometimes find that I’m not used to straightforwardly facing my own family issues,” she says. “Sometimes I just move forward through life. During this process, I saw the different perspectives of the different sisters, the younger one and the elder one, and also myself, my own perspective.” The new outlook is a continuation of her ever-evolving view of her own sisters as she’s grown into adulthood. She’s started to see her sisters as their own individuals, outside of her own perspective as merely younger and older sisters. It’s an observation she likely wouldn’t have made in her younger days: “In the past, when I was still a student, I think I was more egocentric and more of a rebel.” Yeh went to work in Korea a decade ago, still a teenager, having trained for two years before she made her K-pop debut. She says working at such a young age made her grow up faster than her sisters. “Sometimes when I go back to see my elder sister, I sometimes feel like she’s kind of childish,” she says, lovingly taking a jab at her older sibling. “Growing up brought me a different way of perceiving my sisters.” She’s noticed that her younger sister, on the other hand, has changed in the years she’s been away. “I can see she’s also becoming more mature and more considerate to other people,” she says. Yeh’s still active as a K-pop idol, even if she’s about to make her TIFF debut as an actress. She and I-dle released new music earlier this year, and the group experienced one of the most significant stages of their career this summer, performing at Chicago’s Lollapalooza. The other women of I-dle — Miyeon, Minnie, Soyeon and Yuqi — have been by her side throughout every major moment of her career, including her move into acting. “My members know that taking part in a film has been one of my deepest wishes, and they always wish me the best of luck,” Yeh says. The other members of I-dle will often ask to see clips of the movie or anything she can share with them. Yeh’s a bit nervous for them to see the final product, especially since at the time of this Zoom conversation she had yet to see it herself. Yeh performs onstage during Lollapalooza at Grant Park on July 31, 2026. Joshua Applegate/WireImage Yeh’s quick to admit she’s not afraid to be in front of the camera or in the spotlight — it becomes second nature when it’s part of your daily life, one has to imagine. But the thought of standing onstage at her own movie premiere has her feeling something new. “When I start to imagine that I’m standing on the ground of TIFF, I don’t actually feel nervous,” she says. “But as the days are coming closer — I’ve started to see all the marketing and the press talking about this — it’s been a constant reminder that it’s happening. It’s really happening.” Still, “nerves” isn’t quite the word she would use to describe how she’s feeling. “Instead of being nervous, I would say my heart’s pounding for it. I feel excited, and I really would like to embrace this experience.” Yeh’s hoping audiences at TIFF and beyond will embrace Happily Ever After too. This film and this story, she says, have deeply touched her and the rest of the cast and crew. She’s hoping that will resonate with a global audience. She also has a more selfish wish — that audiences will see more than just Shuhua the K-pop idol and be open to the fact that she’s trying something she loves. Says Yeh: “I hope, of course, that the audiences can finally see me as an actress. I constantly encourage myself to grow in terms of self-discovery and challenge myself. I won’t let myself down.” THR

title: ‘Look Back’ Breakouts Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada on Growing Up on a Hirokazu Koreeda Set
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada Courtesy of Getty Images Like the characters they would ultimately play, child actors Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada could easily have become rivals when they first arrived on the set of Japanese auteur Hirokazu Koreeda ‘s latest acclaimed drama, Look Back . Both 11-year-old fifth graders when filming began, the two actresses came to the film with opposite levels of experience and very different dispositions. Okada had been appearing in Japanese film and TV projects since she was an infant. “I’ve been working in this business since before I could even understand things, so it’s like everyday life to me now,” she says. The young veteran was chosen for her role for her layered poise and Koreeda’s confidence that she was up to the task of mastering the dialect of Japan’s remote Akita prefecture, the place her character would call home. Nanase, meanwhile, was a total newcomer to the screen who had been scouted and picked purely on the basis of her natural, bubbly charisma and seemingly boundless confidence. Related Stories Movies Toronto Awards Analysis: 'I Play Rocky' Channels Namesake, Could Follow in Its Oscar Footsteps Movies 'Misty Green' Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is a Revelation in Chris Rock's Sharply Observed Love-Hate Portrait of the Hollywood Hustle “I remember looking at her on the first day and thinking, Hmm, is she really so good?” says Nanase. “But then we were introduced and started talking, and I was like, wow, this girl is really interesting!” The pair, who later shared their 12th birthdays on set just one day apart, became instant best buds. By the time of Look Back ‘s well-received world premiere in Venice last week, they had grown inseparable. As a duo, they landed on various fashion outlets’ best-dressed-of-the-festival lists, thanks to their stylishly retro outfits and adorable antics on the red carpet, where they struck coordinated poses and jumped in the air in unison. The Hollywood Reporter caught up with Nanase and Okada on the Lido the following day for what amounted to their very first interview with the international press. “I can’t imagine how I could have gotten through this whole experience without her by my side,” says Okada. “I think I would have been really scared, but instead it has been so fun together.” Furi Nanase and Rokka Okada in ‘Look Back’ Among Japan’s most decorated contemporary directors, Koreeda’s great hallmark, aside from the gentle humanism of his storytelling, is the unforgettable work he consistently gets from child actors. His 2004 breakthrough, the child-abandonment drama Nobody Knows , would see its 12-year-old star Yuya Yagira take home the Cannes Film Festival’s best actor award, making him the youngest winner in the festival’s history. Much of the director’s most feted work that has followed has hinged upon delicately naturalistic performances from kids, from the switched-at-birth saga Like Father, Like Son (Cannes’ jury prize winner in 2013) to his Palme d’Or triumph, Shoplifters (2018), and recent best screenplay winner, Monster (2023). Nanase says she wasn’t sure what to expect for her audition with Koreeda and his producers, because they hadn’t sent her any scenes to prepare. Instead, they said she should just come to the meeting and be herself. “The moment he entered the room, he had this aura of someone who takes his time and has everything under control, which was very comforting,” Nanase remembers. “He spoke to me like I was a grown-up person, but he was very kind and gentle.” Later, on set, Koreeda would explain each scene to his inexperienced star and then give her the dialog shortly before rolling cameras. “He would share the main idea behind the scene and tell me what he would like me to do,” she says. “But then he would say, ‘What do you think about this? Do you think it’s a good idea? Is there anything else you want to try?'” Nanase adds: “Before we started, I was a little worried about how everything would feel on set, but it never once made me nervous.” Before preproduction, Koreeda’s only request to his actors was that they not read the manga (Japanese comic) on which Look Back is based, nor watch the popular anime of the same name that was previously adapted from it. Instead, Koreeda’s team suggested they watch Shoplifters and Monster with their parents, to give them a sense of the endeavor they were joining. “Both films had something in them that sticks in your heart, something that you don’t find in normal movies,” says Okada. “I thought they were beautiful.” Look Back is a feature adaptation of Japanese artist Tatsuki Fujimoto’s wildly popular manga of the same name. A coming-of-age drama of delicate simplicity, the story follows Fujino (played by newcomer Nanase), a vivacious grade-schooler whose gift at drawing comic strips has made her a minor celebrity at her small-town elementary school in remote northern Japan. Fujino’s budding drive to become a great artist is further inflamed when she sees the drawings of Kyomoto (Okada), a reclusive classmate who rarely leaves home but whose work has a surprisingly adult-like sophistication. What begins as a fierce rivalry between the two eventually blossoms into an adoring friendship and manga-making partnership — Fujino draws the characters, Kyomoto does backgrounds — as the story follows the two girls over 13 years as they come of age, get a first taste of professional publishing success, and eventually experience a heartbreaking falling out that sends them down separate paths. Shot on location in Japan’s northern Tohoku region over the course of a full year, the film is positively Studio Ghibli-esque in its reverent portrayal of childhood innocence in the Japanese countryside — amid the shifting beauty of the seasons and the halting wonders and dramas of growing up. Midway through the film, adult actresses Natsuki Deguchi and Aju Makita, who bear an uncanny resemblance to the kids, step in to play the more mature Fujino and Kyomoto. The only in-depth preparation the project required of its younger stars, aside from dialect coaching for Okada, was intensive drawing practice. As in the film, Nanase was trained to draw figures, while Okada learned to sketch backgrounds and panoramas. Koreeda brought the two on a shopping outing to a bookshop in Tokyo where they bought loads of drawing books and materials, and later they took online drawing classes and met regularly with a professional manga artist. “All of the directors I’ve worked with so far have always been very nice to me, but director Koreeda is on another level,” says Okada. “He is so good at giving advice. I remember when we were shooting one of the first drawing scenes together, he told us to focus all our attention on the sound of our pens scratching the paper, like it’s music, and that was somehow very helpful.” Above all, Look Back is a story about the making of artists, and the film’s two young leads say they intend to carry some of that spirit into the next stage of their careers. “My character, Fujino, has so much determination once she decides she wants to become a manga artist, and that’s how I want to be too,” says Nanase. “I’ll be carrying her with me when I go to my next audition — absolute confidence!” Okada, despite her lifelong acting background, says Look Back has similarly changed how she thinks about her path. “Kyomoto is able to look inside herself and think deeply about what kind of artist she wants to become,” says the 12-year-old. “I want to try to do that too — so I can try to reach higher and higher with my acting.” THR

title: Toronto Awards Analysis: ‘I Play Rocky’ Channels Namesake, Could Follow in Its Oscar Footsteps
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By Scott Feinberg Plus Icon Scott Feinberg Executive Editor of Awards ScottFeinberg Follow Sign Up View All September 12, 2026 10:18pm Anthony Ippolito in 'I Play Rocky' Claire Folger/Amazon Content Services Sometimes, history repeats itself. Exactly a half-century ago, in the year of the American bicentennial, a low-profile film — the story of a small-time boxer who, against all odds, went the distance against the champ — became a gigantic hit and ended up vanquishing the likes of All the President’s Men , Network and Taxi Driver to win the best picture Oscar. That film was John G. Avildsen’s Rocky , which was written by and starred Sylvester Stallone . Eight years ago, another film with a low-profile premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival , where it polarized critics but played through the roof with festivalgoers and ended up winning the TIFF audience award en route to several Oscar nominations, including one for best picture, which it ultimately won. That film was Peter Farrelly ’s Green Book . Related Stories Movies Anthony Ippolito on Speaking to Sylvester Stallone Before Filming 'I Play Rocky': "Very Overwhelming and Daunting" Movies Mahershala Ali Reveals He Was "Yearning" to Perform Action On-Screen Before Filming 'Your Mother, Your Mother, Your Mother' On Saturday night, Farrelly returned to TIFF for the world premiere of I Play Rocky , a film about the inspiration for and making of Rocky . Like Green Book , it polarized critics, but delighted festivalgoers — indeed, it generated numerous instances of mid-film applause, as well as a lengthy standing ovation at the end — and it will probably follow in the footsteps of Rocky and Green Book to a best picture Oscar nom, if not a win. If nothing else, I Play Rocky will catapult its little-known star, Anthony Ippolito , who plays Stallone, into the thick of a crowded best actor Oscar race. The 27-year-old eerily channels Sly’s unconventional but iconic appearance and manner of speaking, and, as was the case with Stallone 50 years ago, the story of his path to his career-changing part will have many rooting for him as much as the character he plays. Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky’ Claire Folger/Amazon MGM Studios The biggest hazard for I Play Rocky , which Amazon/MGM is set to begin rolling out in the U.S. on Nov. 6, is Stallone himself. In THR ’s TIFF lounge , Ippolito said he had spoken with Stallone before playing him and Farrelly said he had shown Stallone the finished film and Stallone was pleased with it. And during remarks from the TIFF stage just before the film unspooled, Farrelly gave a shout out to Stallone. But Stallone was not directly involved with — nor does it seems he will financially benefit from — I Play Rocky . title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Review: Peter Farrelly’s Sensational Biopic Of The Making Of Stallone’s Classic Is Just As Inspiring As The Original Movie – Toronto Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is The Whole Show In Chris Rock’s Sizzling Hollywood Portrait Of A Down-And-Out Emmy Winner Whose Career Is On The Skids – Toronto Film Festival ‘The Surgeon’ Review: Michelle Yeoh Goes All John Wick Taking Her Scalpel To The Bad Guys – Toronto Film Festival ‘Closing Night’ Review: Killer Cast Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts And Dianne Wiest As Mothers On The Edge – Toronto Film Festival View All September 12, 2026 9:30pm Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone in 'I Play Rocky' Amazon MGM It is no spoiler to say I am going to reveal the final moments of Peter Farrelly ‘s fantastic crowd-pleasing biopic I Play Rocky , chronicling the making of the 1976 classic Rocky , which not only made Sylvester Stallone a major star but also became one of the greatest behind-the-scenes stories in Hollywood history. Stay all the way through the very last of the credits and you will be rewarded with the only scene in this saga not re-created for the movie. Introducing Stallone for the first time on The Tonight Show to promote Rocky, Johnny Carson tells a bit of the incredible backstory of Stallone turning down hundreds of thousands of dollars for his screenplay in order to insist he star in the movie he wrote for himself (even though he was completely unknown at the time). “If someone were to actually make a movie about the making of Rocky nobody would believe it,” Carson prophetically said. Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Festivals The Obsession For The Next ‘Obsession’ At TIFF: Festival Hot List Includes Pics For Sale With Cynthia Erivo, Chase Infiniti, The Maras, Dave Bautista & More Well, someone has done that, and the film that has resulted is a winner in every way, a movie that in fact manages to carry the same emotional wallop as the original Rocky and containing a performance from Anthony Ippolito that is so uncanny I didn’t for a minute think he was anyone but the actual Stallone. It feels like they just used de-aging technology so Stallone could play himself a half-century younger. But make no mistake, Ippolito’s powerful, moving and inspiring portrayal is not mere imitation. This guy inhabits Stallone in every way, delivering an authentic portrait that will blow you away. Watch on Deadline Farrelly has said he would not have made the film without Stallone’s blessing, which he got, and he has, with Peter Gamble’s beautifully structured and crafted screenplay, made one of the best movies ever made about Hollywood moviemaking and the sheer mechanics of getting anything made. Certainly it is one of the most entertaining. In a year that marks the 50th anniversary of Rocky, a film that spawned five sequels and three more films in the Creed spinoff series with Michael B. Jordan, I Play Rocky brings us full circle right back to the beginning and manages to slyly recapture the fresh spirit that birthed it. This film has turned the making of Rocky into its own Rocky-like moment of triumph. Starting with Ippolito on screen as “Mike Stallone” auditioning for a nameless role, one of those aspiring actors working any menial job he can to support his dreams of making it in the industry, Gamble’s script shows us in linear fashion exactly how this impossible dream happened. From scraping the bottom of the barrel, even doing soft porn (a hilarious audition scene that really happened), finding a puppy he names Butkus, meeting his eventual wife Sasha (a perfect AnnaSophia Robb) at the movie theater where he works, and finally getting a break to meet big-time producers Irwin Winkler (PJ Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell) who sadly inform him Jan Michael Vincent got the job so the role of his brother has to go to someone else, all the ups and downs of the life of an actor trying to just get by and keep going are here. On his way out the door of their office he tucks a script he wrote called Paradise Alley (eventually a movie Stallone got made) under a pile that says “weekend reading.” Their assistant knew the ruse but read the script and praised it, which caught the producers’ attention. They tell him he has real talent as a writer and to come up with some ideas. Sitting at a bar wondering how he was going to get by he sees a Muhammed Ali fight and bingo, the idea for Rocky comes pouring out of him, written in longhand in only three and a half days and handed to Sasha to type. Chartoff/Winkler (Byrne and Kebbell are really wonderful in these parts) sparks to it and manage to sell to a skeptical studio head, Sandy Maddux (a terrific and scene-stealing Tracy Letts in a composite of studio execs at the time). “Boxing pictures? Nobody makes boxing pictures,” he barks. The only hang-up is Stallone won’t sell it to them unless he stars in it. In a series of scenes where the price keeps going up with seemingly no ceiling, Sly holds his ground. “I won’t sell it for $1 million. Not $10 million,” he swears, and you can see the passion of a man who believes in himself, willing to “go the distance” just like Rocky to prove it. Finally, after knocking the budget down to just $1 million with clauses designed to get Stallone fired so they can get Ryan O’Neal or an actor on that level when it inevitably falls behind schedule, the saga of the actual filming begins and it has all been re-created with tender loving care, from the cinematography to production design, costume, music, editing and one riotous scene after another. It is not just about the making of this one film against all odds, but rather it is really about the making of just about every film, a love letter to movies that in its own way is on par with Truffaut’s Day For Night. A scene in Philadelphia at the meat-packing plant where they find the local union head has gotten wind they are shooting without permits turns into an amusing nail-biting moment where all the equipment and cast and crew has to be immediately hidden before he gets there. Another scene, the re-creation of the iconic run up the Philly steps, show us one of the first uses ever of the now indispensable Steadicam (using the original, I am told) as it reinvented that aspect of moviemaking. But the emotional knockout is delivered in the filming of a scene with Burgess Meredith (played by Robert Morgan) as Mickey, who tells Rockey he will agree to train him, after first rejecting him. The key scene just wasn’t working, and director John Avildsen (a great Jay Duplass) tells him they have to do it again, but how? It needs a stronger emotional hook or it fails. Stallone then proceeded to completely make up a five-minute take on the spot that is masterfully delivered. Ippolito brought me to tears watching him play it, quite tricky since this improv is now scripted but has to feel spontaneous. The entire cast with Ippolito is ideal, with special shoutouts to Keki Seto as Talia Shire and Stephan James as Carl Weathers, both taking on Stallone’s iconic Rocky co-stars in style. There are so many highlights in a movie that pulls off a tall task in bringing the same feeling we got the first time we saw Rocky. Farrelly, who won and deserved a couple of Oscars including Best Picture for Green Book, a film that tugs at the heartstrings without ever being anything less than simply human, has now made another film that makes us feel good about life and ourselves. Like Frank Capra used to do, he has made a movie that gives us hope. It couldn’t come at a better time. Producers are Toby Emmerich, Christian Baha, Farrelly, Paul Currie and Michele Weiss. title: ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is a Revelation in Chris Rock’s Sharply Observed Love-Hate Portrait of the Hollywood Hustle
full_text: × Skip to main content The Sports Issue: Uniting the Biggest Names in Hollywood With the Athletes They Admire Most close By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 12, 2026 8:30pm Rosalind Eleazar in 'Misty Green.' Courtesy of TIFF The title characer in Chris Rock ’s sure-footed fourth feature as director, Misty Green , is having a rough week. An actress still best known for a TV series that ended years back, she’s about to be evicted, her bipolar brother is fresh out of a psych ward and in need of both emotional and financial support, a pimpy former colleague dangles a lucrative sex-work gig, and while her undeniable gifts might very well help her book an acting job, the many axes she has to grind in the entertainment industry keep getting in the way. In a star-making performance, Rosalind Eleazar — best known as the tough MI5 operative grieving for her partner on Slow Horses — bites into this gift of a role with grit, tenacity and zero-fucks-given scrappiness. It’s a revelatory turn in a sensitively observed drama that depicts Los Angeles as both a shimmering beacon of fame and success and a soul-sucking grind of constant rejection, where disparities of race, class and gender are as much an obstacle as that casting director who seems to hate you. Following its premieres at the Toronto and New York film festivals, A24 will release the movie Oct. 9. Related Stories Movies 'The Surgeon' Review: Michelle Yeoh Plays a Kidnapped Doctor Trying to Outwit Her Captors in Deliriously Fun Genre-Bender Movies Mahershala Ali Reveals He Was "Yearning" to Perform Action On-Screen Before Filming 'Your Mother, Your Mother, Your Mother' Misty Green The Bottom Line Simultaneously breezy and steeped in melancholy. Venue : Toronto International Film Festival (Gala Presentations) Release date : Friday, Oct. 9 Cast : Rosalind Eleazar, Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick, Chris Rock, Topher Grace, Alexandra Shipp, Amy Landecker, Tracie Thoms, Necar Zadegan, Rich Sommer Director-screenwriter : Chris Rock Rated R, 1 hour 44 minutes Coming 12 years after Rock’s last feature as writer-director, Top Five , a highly entertaining account of the quest to be taken seriously of a standup comic with a history of substance abuse issues, Misty Green is both an extension of certain themes explored in the 2014 film and a departure. While Andre Allen, Rock’s character in the earlier movie, had a fear of not being funny when sober, Eleazar’s Misty is more of a dabbler than an addict. But her problems with impulse control make it hard for her to say no to a night of hard partying, which tends to mess with her professional obligations. The biggest difference, however, is that Misty Green is a significantly more mellow and thoughtful movie, the work of a mature director who knows what he wants to say and has full command of the tone of voice in which to say it. The film is frequently funny, but Rock and his actors never push for comedy. The wry humor is undergirded by melancholy, darkness, despair — by an awareness that even when you appear to have made it in Hollywood, maintaining that perch on the success ladder is not a given. Talent alone often is not enough. Misty appears to have been floundering for years, bristling every time some young up-and-comer tells her how much their mom and dad loved her in her Emmy-winning role on a show called Red Eye . She’s handed a deadline to pull herself out of her rut when Celine (Amy Landecker, hilariously caustic) bursts in unannounced to kick Misty out of her late husband’s apartment. Dazed and hungover, Misty protests that Celine’s husband gave her the apartment, but the unmerry widow is not buying it, giving her a week to find new digs. The industry town’s monomania makes it seem almost normal when Celine starts running audition lines with her before begrudgingly agreeing to the seven-day grace period. With no money and no friends or exes willing to help her out, Misty needs to book a role, pronto. But given her abrasive reputation — she was once fired off a film for punching the wardrobe woman in the face — that’s not easy. Things are further complicated by the reappearance of her loose-cannon brother Jay ( Daniel Kaluuya ), released from a psych ward but still only tenuously in control of his mental health. Her occasional hook-up, the slick and insincere Zach ( Adam Driver ), tempts her out on the town the night before an important audition, offering her a chance at big money if she’s willing to put aside her moral qualms and be part of the “entertainment” for a frisky emir at a lavish party in Dubai. Driver has often been fearless about playing unlikable characters, but Zach takes him to new lows of douchiness when he’s tossing Birkin bags, jewels and cash to a screaming crowd of paid models. Her least complicated relationship is with straight-talking bestie Naomi ( Anna Kendrick ), with whom she works out at a gym near the Santa Monica Pier. Naomi serves as a sounding board and support system for Misty’s anxieties. That’s more than she gets from her agent Randy ( Topher Grace ), who throws up his hands in defeat after another abortive audition, telling her, “No one wants to work with you. You’re too difficult!” While this is very much an ensemble piece, with a bright constellation around Eleazar’s blazing supernova, Rock gives himself a choice suporting role as the one person in the industry who might not have given up on Misty. Jordan is a director who was forced to fire Misty some years back for her anger issues. He’s now staying in her apartment building while holding auditions for a Dreamgirls remake, and while he’s wary about working with the volatile Misty again, he doesn’t rule it out. That remains true even after she gets high with Zach while on an impromtpu date with Jordan, getting them both banged up in a car accident. She goes back to her apartment — where the eviction clock keeps ticking — and tips her stash of booze and pills down the drain, probably not for the first time, but maybe the last? Jordan often gets to channel classic Rock humor (“All civil rights movies suck, you wanna know how I know? Because white people like them!”), but the character is also notable for his sensitivity, even soulfulness. Jordan is an industry veteran with genuine empathy for people like Misty, coughed up and spat out while trying to sustain a career in the face of endless closed doors. The chemistry of Eleazar’s scenes with Rock is sublime. Eleazar’s layered, brittle but also vulnerable performance makes Misty’s depths as a performer apparent, notably in two songs. She sings with moving expressiveness on a torchy version of “One Night Only” in her Dreamgirls audition and a stunningly heartfelt take on Radiohead’s “Creep,” in a Hollywood Roosevelt lounge bar gig. Naturally, her propensity for self-sabotage means her path is one step forward, two steps back, through no fault of her own when Jay loses his cool after being pulled over twice by the same Black cop (Anthony Anderson, one of a handful of cameos) in both cases with no cause beyond racial profiling. When Jay lands in prison, the fiercely protective Misty feels obligated to come up with his exorbitant bail, prompting desperate choices that nudge her career goals aside. Throughout all this, Eleazar keeps us firmly in Misty’s corner in a bold performance that simultaneously pushes the audience away while pulling us in. The tenderness with which Rock has built this vehicle around character, actress and a milieu he clearly knows intimately imbue the material with an aching depth of feeling that stayed with me for days. Misty Green is a poignant snapshot of one woman sweating on the showbiz treadmill, in a town where glittering dreams, crushing defeat and emergency compromise solutions often walk in tandem — the latter echoed in constant local crime news reports heard on car radios. Misty’s personality flaws are what make her so captivating in a smart, refreshingly understated movie that’s very much an insider’s view — jaded, but also clear-eyed — and a credit especially to Rock and Eleazar. Sengupta, Miles Alva Director of photography: Kira Kelly Production designer: Michelle Patterson Costume designer: Neishea Lemle Music: Marcus Miller Editor: Adam Dicterow Casting: Victoria Thomas Rated R, 1 hour 44 minutes THR

title: ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is The Whole Show In Chris Rock’s Sizzling Hollywood Portrait Of A Down-And-Out Emmy Winner Whose Career Is On The Skids – Toronto Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is The Whole Show In Chris Rock’s Sizzling Hollywood Portrait Of A Down-And-Out Emmy Winner Whose Career Is On The Skids – Toronto Film Festival ‘The Surgeon’ Review: Michelle Yeoh Goes All John Wick Taking Her Scalpel To The Bad Guys – Toronto Film Festival ‘Closing Night’ Review: Killer Cast Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts And Dianne Wiest As Mothers On The Edge – Toronto Film Festival View All September 12, 2026 8:30pm Rosalind Eleazar in 'Misty Green' A24/Youtube. I have to confess I am a sucker for down-on-your-luck Hollywood stories, especially movies about actresses who once had success and are now scraping the bottom. Of course there is the classic of classics, Sunset Boulevard, but there are many more. A personal favorite is The Star, which got Bette Davis an Academy Award nomination as a has-been who walks around Hollywood carrying her Oscar saying things like “Come on Oscar. Let’s go get drunk.” Jane Fonda got nominated as well playing a down-and-outer in Hollywood in The Morning After. For sleazy fun, there’s Connie Stevens in The Sex Symbol, Kim Novak in The Legend of Lylah Clare (“Tell them Lylah is coming!”), and a great Natalie Wood in a real favorite Inside Daisy Clover to name just a handful. The lure of Hollywood and the dark side of those who chase the dream has been fascinating subject matter for filmmakers throughout Hollywood history and now it is Chris Rock ‘s turn. Rock was doing a group voice-over session and noticed a couple of once successful actresses from hit sitcoms who were now doing this kind of day work to keep the lights on and it got him thinking about a scenario that eventually became his latest idea for a film, Misty Green . It has been 12 years since his last and most critically acclaimed turn behind the lens with 2014’s Top Five. Earlier this century he tried his hand directing 2003’s Head of State and 2007’s I Think I Love My Wife (I quite liked that one), though neither of those two were box office hits. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews News How Meditation, Hope And Hard Work Brought Rosalind Eleazar Her “Long Shot” Dream Lead In Chris Rock’s ‘Misty Green’ Now he is back, and if Misty Green will be remembered for anything it is the remarkable performance of British actress Rosalind Eleazar , a co-star currently on Slow Horses but soon who will be known as well for playing the title role in this story of an L.A.-based television actress, a once-upon-a-time Supporting Actress Emmy winner, now going through tough times, various addictions, family problems and standing in her own way of reviving her career because she won’t lower herself to audition. This is the kind of material that could lend itself to show business clichés (we have seen it a hundred times), but Rock has created a character, specifically a Black actress on the skids, the kind we don’t get to see portrayed on screen as opposed to the long list of similar stories listed above with white stars. This is all about Misty. We meet her best friend Naomi ( Anna Kendrick ), who tries to encourage her, even helping with a self-tape audition Misty resists; we meet her frustrated agent Randy ( Topher Grace ), who complains because on the last job she punched a co-star; we meet friend and would-be filmmaker Zach ( Adam Driver ), whose drug-induced invitations and sleazy job ops are not what Misty needs but can’t resist because she needs the cash; and we meet her brother Jay ( Daniel Kaluuya ), whose is in and out of jail, a mess, but someone she loves and wants to help. These are the people around her and they also include Jordan (Rock plays him), a working director with whom she has a past, and with whom she might have a future dream role if she can get her act together. Misty Green is also a pretty depressing portrait of L.A., the land of the haves and the have nots as Rock sees it, a fairly empty place dreamers head towards with no idea how to navigate a life worth living. Really this scenario isn’t particularly fresh, but I have to say when I heard the brief synopsis I was all in. It is a bit uneven though in execution, and Rock, in his role, plays it seriously until resorting to some dialogue and use of the N-word that resembles his old stand-up rather the guy he’s playing here. But is all lifted way up high by Eleazar, who makes this all worth the ticket. She’s mesmerizing in one of the best performances by an actress this year. You believe her; you may even know her. Among the rest of the cast the standout is Kaluuya, who is heartbreaking as a young man who simply has never been able to get out of his own way, despite the best intentions. Driver gets the sleaze of his role just right, though it is a one-dimensional character. In the large cast there are some familiar walk-ons such as Anthony Anderson as a cop, and even Ice T as himself. The Los Angeles locations are well chosen, giving a sense of what the city really is behind the fake glamour. Rock is a very smart performer, you can’t have doubts about that, and he has a keen eye for the underbelly of showbiz. So even in a movie that is not the sum of all its parts, many of those parts are pretty good and he has delivered a film that will be remembered as the one that gave us a glimpse of the movie star Rosalind Eleazar is about to become. Producers are Peter Rice, Rock, Victoria Thomas and David Worthen Brooks. title: FCC Chairman Brendan Carr Accuses James Talarico Of Running A “Hoax” With Jimmy Kimmel Sit-Down; YouTube Interview Nears 7 Million Views
full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Anthropic CEO Calls For Slowing Down AI Development, Warns Of “Swarm” Taking Over Internet In 6-12 Months CBS Wants Ex-‘Matlock’ Writer’s Racial & Sexual Harassment Suit Dismissed; Says Claims Are “Fabrications & Outright Lies” Jimmy Kimmel’s James Talarico Interview Posted To YouTube As Host Calls Out Trump And FCC: “They Want To Make Our Editorial Decisions For Us” View All September 12, 2026 7:09pm Brendan Carr Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images As Jimmy Kimmel ‘s interview with James Talarico nears 7 million views on YouTube, FCC chairman Brendan Carr weighed in on Saturday evening, accusing the Texas U.S. Senate candidate of orchestrating a “hoax” to drive up “clicks and donations.” Earlier this week, Kimmel told viewers that he would be sitting down with an interview with Talarico for his ABC late-night show, but that it would be posted to YouTube and not broadcast because of the FCC’s crackdown on its equal time rule . In a post on X, Carr accused Talarico of “just running the same hoax he did a few months ago on Colbert for the purpose of getting clicks and donations — he’s banking on people not understanding the statute or operating as partisan lemmings.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Anthropic CEO Calls For Slowing Down AI Development, Warns Of "Swarm" Taking Over Internet In 6-12 Months Predictions Pete Hammond's Primetime Emmy Predictions: 'Widow's Bay' Possible Record, 'Hacks' Spoiler, 'The Pitt', 'DTF St. Louis', Colbert/Kimmel Combo He also posted a meme of Talarico riding on a bicycle on Kimmel’s back before Kimmel puts a stick in the spokes and it crashes to the ground. Ok, fine. I’ll weigh in. 1. The Equal Time statute doesn’t apply to GameDay for several reasons. For one, when it passed the statute, Congress applied it to broadcast tv stations—not cable programs like GameDay. For another, Congress stated that the statute only applies to… https://t.co/r3KP7RvQL8 pic.twitter.com/m5IbEl8Ngr — Brendan Carr (@BrendanCarrFCC) September 13, 2026 A Talarico campaign spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Kimmel interview had drawn 6.8 million views as of Saturday evening. In February, Stephen Colbert posted an interview with Talarico to YouTube, telling viewers that he was warned by network executives about featuring the candidate on the broadcast. That interview generated 9.6 million views on YouTube. Like the Kimmel interview, the YouTube views were well over the average audience for the actual late-night broadcast. In an interview this week, Talarico characterized the Kimmel incident as government censorship and a form of “cancel culture.” He also posted the interview to X, calling it “the interview Trump’s FCC doesn’t want you to see.” For decades, daytime and late-night TV talk shows have operated on the assumption that they were exempt from the FCC’s equal time rule, which requires broadcasters who feature candidates to provide comparable time to their rivals, if it is requested. News coverage and news interviews have been exempt from the requirements, and the rule also does not apply cable or streaming, where the FCC’s authority is limited. But in January, the FCC under Carr , appointed by Donald Trump , issued guidance to broadcasters that TV talk shows actually may not be exempt, a move that critics saw as a regulatory effort to crack down on daytime and late-night hosts the president does not like. Within weeks, the agency launched an investigation of ABC’s The View after it featured Talarico as a guest. Until now, Carr had yet to weigh in on Kimmel’s latest criticisms and the decision to move the interview to YouTube. The late night host called the FCC’s equal time enforcement threats an effort to “make our editorial decisions for us, which of course we cannot accept.” On Thursday, a White House spokesperson said that Kimmel was “play acting” to “create a false narrative,” and that Carr “has not threatened him regarding interviewing James Talarico , or any other candidate.” Carr has denied that the FCC’s stricter enforcement of the equal time rule was an attempt to censor guests. On X, Carr posted, “The Equal Time statute does not prohibit anyone from interviewing anyone on broadcast tv. It is about more speech, not less. Congress wanted to ensure that voters would decide elections, not media gatekeepers picking winners and losers by providing preferential airtime to some candidates and not others. Indeed, when the statute applies, it simply requires broadcast stations to offer comparable time and placement. And comparable does not necessarily mean an interview by the same person on the same program either.” Carr’s comments were in response to a post from University of Texas Democrats, who noted the appearance of Sen. Ted Cruz (D-TX) on ESPN’s College GameDay on Saturday. The group posted on X, “So I can’t watch Talarico on Kimmel but I have to watch Ted Cruz on GameDay?” The FCC chairman noted that the equal time rule would not apply to Cruz’s appearance because it was on a cable network and because the regulation covers only legal qualified candidates, or contenders who are in the midst of an election campaign. Cruz is not up for reelection this year; Talarico’s Republican rival is Ken Paxton. ABC is challenging the FCC’s enforcement of the rule when it comes to The View, pointing out that the agency affirmed its exemption from the regulation in a 2002 letter. The network also has sued the FCC on First Amendment grounds. It claims that the agency’s order that its eight owned stations submit to early license renewals is a form of regulatory retaliation, due to the Trump administration’s dislike of its news coverage and other content including The View and Kimmel. In his post, Carr again defended the FCC’s regulatory efforts as within the bounds of the agency’s authority. He wrote, “In exchange for that free and exclusive right to use spectrum, broadcasters made a deal with the American people. They agreed to operate, not in their own narrow interests, but in the public interest. There are various rules and policies that they must follow. This sets them apart from newspapers and cable shows and podcasts. But some broadcasters want to break their deal with the American people. They want to keep their free access to billions of dollars worth of spectrum, of course. They are less eager these days to abide by their public interest obligations.” ABC’s legal team has argued that the FCC is engaging in selective enforcement, as its January guidance did not target conservative talk radio, and wrote that the equal time rule is unworkable for shows like The View as it puts network stations on the hook for time to potentially dozens of candidates on the ballot. Kimmel said this week that he would love to interview Paxton, but “our affiliates in Texas would have to give equal time to as many candidates as there are on the ballot. title: ‘The Surgeon’ Review: Michelle Yeoh Goes All John Wick Taking Her Scalpel To The Bad Guys – Toronto Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Misty Green’ Review: Rosalind Eleazar Is The Whole Show In Chris Rock’s Sizzling Hollywood Portrait Of A Down-And-Out Emmy Winner Whose Career Is On The Skids – Toronto Film Festival ‘The Surgeon’ Review: Michelle Yeoh Goes All John Wick Taking Her Scalpel To The Bad Guys – Toronto Film Festival ‘Closing Night’ Review: Killer Cast Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts And Dianne Wiest As Mothers On The Edge – Toronto Film Festival View All September 12, 2026 7:05pm Michelle Yeoh in 'The Surgeon' Toronto International Film Festival After supporting roles in blockbusters like Wicked , Michelle Yeoh has her first all-out starring role since winning the Best Actress Oscar for Everything Everywhere All at Once three years ago. Considering her expertise in martial arts and kick-ass action ( Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon for starters), her latest effort in the genre is a lot of fun but not for squeamish stomachs since The Surgeon makes The Pitt look like PAW Patrol. This medical thrill ride holds nothing back in exploring the human anatomy as weaponry that even John Wick would envy. Maybe we should call this one John Sick ? Who needs a gun when you bring on instant death just by pulling out the colon and squeezing for 30 seconds. This movie from writer-director Dr. Roshan Sethi (A Nice Indian Boy) is a manual for turning bad guys inside out – literally. There can be no doubt what attracted Yeoh, a supreme action star as well as serious actor, to the role of Eliza, a world-renowned surgeon who has followed her Monastic code of medicine for 40 years and now is retiring. Early on a phone call from her insurance company says it all: “Should we continue insuring your hands?” and the answer is no, no longer necessary. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews Toronto Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews Festivals The Obsession For The Next ‘Obsession’ At TIFF: Festival Hot List Includes Pics For Sale With Cynthia Erivo, Chase Infiniti, The Maras, Dave Bautista & More But those plans to take it all easy are rudely interrupted when she is abducted at gunpoint by criminals and ordered to operate on their gravely ill leader, Sean ( Martin Freeman ). Apparently she is the only hope this crime boss has, and his henchmen, notably Cole (Yuri Kolokolnikov), an imposing Russian bad guy, is watching closely to make sure she does what she is ordered to do as she cuts him open, starts removing organs, and proceeds to make the weakest among us want to reach for the barf bag. Prosthetics supervisor Suzi Battersby leaves little to the imagination. Congratulations, Suzi. Eliza senses once she has done the job she will be killed, but they have come to play with the wrong doc. She does make one demand: that they crank up the Thin Lizzy songs, her preferred music to cut by. It doesn’t take long before she uses her exceptional ability to turn every key body part into a death sentence, particularly in a clock-ticking demonstration of how lethal her hands can be when she sets about slicing and dicing with her scalpel. Yeoh’s martial arts skills really come into play in battling these guys by manipulating their mobility in delightfully paralyzing ways. We get a little more info on Sean in a flashback to her initial meeting with him where they talked about his dire diagnosis and knew she was likely his only ticket to live. So how could he accept she had hung up her scrubs? In the tight 92-minute running time, Sethi shows his own bona fides by making a truly original action flick that may be the most informative trip inside the body since Fantastic Voyage. Although Freeman creates a fairly dimensional character while the other baddies are strictly stereotypes, it is Yeoh that makes this enterprise worth watching. She not only still have the action chops, she is completely believable and authentic as a doctor who has seen it all and possesses extraordinary talent in the profession. Her last stand in the operating room is one to behold. Shout-out to fight choreographer Laurent Demanioff for the dazzling moves. There can be no doubt this film, which had its world premiere tonight at the Toronto Film Festival, is a tailor-made vehicle guaranteed to turn up the temperature for Yeoh fans everywhere all at once. Producers are Basil Iwanyk, Erica Lee, Diarmaid McGrath, Tim Headington, Lia Buman, Neil Shah, Steve Klinsky, Adam Kolbrenner, John Schoenfelder and Russell Ackerman.
